units.title: Reading longer Russian: participles, gerunds, and the clauses they compress

lessons.title: Participles as a reading tool: recognizing причастия instead of translating them
lessons.explanation: Up to now every verb you have met was finite: it agreed with a subject and carried its own tense. Russian also has a family of verb forms that behave like adjectives, and these are the single biggest reason a real newspaper paragraph can stall a learner who is otherwise fluent at conversation. Cornell groups them honestly: there are six forms derived from verbs (deverbals) that are not listed in a dictionary under their own shape, so you must find the infinitive first and then recognize the form you are looking at. Four of these are declined like adjectives and are called participles (причастие, pree-CHA-stee-ye — participle). The other two are indeclinable, like adverbs, and are called deverbal adverbs or gerunds. This lesson is about the four participles; the next lesson takes the two gerunds. The two families you will meet most are active and passive, and each has a present and a past shape. An active participle describes the noun as doing the action: читающий (chee-TA-yoo-shchee — the one who is reading) and прочитавший (pra-chee-TAF-shee — the one who has read). A passive participle describes the noun as receiving it: читаемый (chee-TA-ye-myy — being read) and прочитанный (pra-CHEE-tan-nyy — read, having been read). The suffixes are stable enough to be worth memorizing as reading cues: -ущ-/-ющ-/-ащ-/-ящ- for the present active, -вш- for the past active, -ем-/-им- for the present passive, and -нн- or -т- for the past passive. Cornell states the key fact plainly: written-style participles equal conversational-style который clauses. That is, читающий человек and человек, который читает both mean 'the person who is reading', but the first belongs to written Russian and the second to speech. So the practical skill is translation by paraphrase: when a participle blocks you, replace it in your head with a который (ka-TO-ryy — who, which) clause and the sentence opens up. Two facts stop the commonest misreadings. First, the names 'present' and 'past' describe how the form is built, not what time it means: a present participle signals action simultaneous with the main verb, so the same form can be translated in the present or the past depending on the main clause. Second, past passive participles look deceptively like deverbal nouns such as открытие (at-KRY-tee-ye — a discovery) beside открытый (at-KRY-tyy — opened).
lessons.example: Read one sentence twice and watch the participle collapse into a clause. Written style: Он говорил с детьми, играющими на улице (on ga-va-REEL s dyet-MEE, ee-GRA-yoo-shchee-mee na OO-lee-tse) — literally 'He spoke with the children playing in the street'. Cornell gives exactly this pair and notes that because the main verb говорил is past, the 'present' participle играющими is translated in English past time: he was talking to the children who were playing outside. Conversational replacement: Он говорил с детьми, которые играли на улице (ka-TO-ryy-ee ee-GRA-lee) — he was talking to the children who were playing outside. Same meaning, spoken register. Now change the participle to the past active: Он говорил с детьми, игравшими на улице (ee-GRAV-shee-mee) — he was talking to the children who had been playing in the street, the -вш- telling you the playing finished before he spoke. Finally the passive: книга, прочитанная нами (KNEE-ga, pra-CHEE-tan-na-ya NA-mee) — the book read by us, which Cornell pairs with книга, которую мы прочитали (ka-TO-roo-yoo my pra-chee-TA-lee). Work through all four, and for each say aloud which noun the participle agrees with and whether that noun is doing or receiving the action, because those two decisions are the whole skill.
lessons.question: A written sentence contains читаемая нами книга. What is the fastest reliable way to understand it, and what does the ending tell you about time?
lessons.answer: Replace the participle with a который clause — книга, которую мы читаем, 'the book which we are reading' — and read the -ем- suffix as present passive built on the non-past stem, signalling action simultaneous with the main verb rather than present time.
lessons.distractor: Read читаемая as a separate past-tense verb meaning 'she read', and translate the phrase as 'the book we read last year'.
lessons.correction: Читаемая cannot be a finite verb: a finite verb would take a person ending and agree with a nominative subject, while -ая is an adjective ending agreeing with книга in the feminine singular. Cornell's present passive participle page shows that this form looks exactly like the non-past мы-form (читаем) plus an adjective ending, and that it is built on imperfective verbs, so it means on-going or repeated action received by the noun. Read the -ем- as passive, not as past, and paraphrase with который читаем to make the meaning transparent.

depth.definitions: A participle is a verb form declined like an adjective. Active means the noun performs the action; passive means the noun receives it. Present and past here name the stem the form is built from — the non-past stem or the past stem — not the moment in time the sentence describes. A deverbal noun is a noun derived from a verb; it is not a participle even when it looks like one. A finite verb is a verb with a person, number and tense, agreeing with a nominative subject.
depth.mechanism: The reason participles exist is compression. Cornell contrasts the two registers directly: written style uses participles, conversational style uses который clauses, and the page summarizing the six forms reduces the whole contrast to 'written style participles = conversational style который clauses'. That single equivalence is why a participle is best learned as a reading device rather than a production target. The mechanism inside a sentence is agreement plus simultaneity. Cornell and Wikipedia both insist that the labels present and past describe formation, not time: the present participle and the present deverbal adverb express action simultaneous with the main verb, so the same participial form is translated in the present when the main verb is present and in the past when the main verb is past. Wikipedia's participle section adds a further limit for reading accuracy: participles are often hard to distinguish from deverbal adjectives, and the active present participle can only be formed from imperfective verbs, so if you meet an -ущ- form you already know the underlying verb was imperfective. None of this needs to be produced under time pressure; all of it needs to be recognized.
depth.secondExample: Contrast the two readings of one form. Sentence one: Он говорит с детьми, играющими на улице (on ga-va-REET s dyet-MEE, ee-GRA-yoo-shchee-mee) — present main verb, so 'He is talking to the children who are playing outside'. Sentence two: Он говорил с детьми, играющими на улице — past main verb, so 'He was talking to the children who were playing outside'. The participle играющими is identical; only the main verb changed, and only the English tense shifted. Cornell prints exactly this pair to make the point. Now put the same content in written compression with a box construction: Он подошёл к стоявшему у двери милиционеру (on pa-da-SHYOL k sta-YAV-she-moo oo DVYE-ree mee-lee-tsa-NYE-roo) — he approached the policeman standing by the door, where стоявшему agrees with милиционеру but the words у двери sit inside the noun phrase. Recognize the agreement and you can move the phrase; try to translate word for word and you get an impossible order. Read the same content in three further shapes, each of which a который clause could replace: the present active phrase стоящий у двери (the one standing by the door), the past active nominal phrase стоявший у двери милиционер (the policeman who had been standing by the door), and приехавший из Москвы (the one who had arrived from Moscow), where the participle agrees with the noun it precedes.
depth.mistake: The commonest error is to read a participle as a finite verb and then hunt for a subject that does not exist, producing a sentence with two verbs and no subject. A second error is to treat 'present participle' as present time and mistranslate a past-time sentence. A third is to confuse a past passive participle with a deverbal noun, so that предложенный (pred-LO-zhen-nyy — proposed) is read as though it were предложение (pred-la-ZHE-nee-ye — a proposal or a sentence). Diagnose by checking the ending first: adjective endings (-ый, -ая, -ое, -ые and their case forms) point to a participle, noun endings point to a noun, and double -нн- belongs to the participial adjective.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: take three sentences you have already met in this course and rewrite each participle as a который clause, then rewrite each который clause back as a participle. Model response for one line: книга, которую мы читаем becomes книга, читаемая нами (KNEE-ga, chee-TA-ye-ma-ya NA-mee) — the book being read by us. Self-review rubric: (1) does the participle agree with the right noun in gender, number and case; (2) did I decide active versus passive from meaning rather than from guessing; (3) did I avoid assigning present time just because the suffix is called present; (4) can I state the который paraphrase aloud without hesitation? Four yes answers mean the form is recognized, not merely translated.
depth.summary: Participles are compressed relative clauses written in adjective clothing. Learn them as recognition devices: find the noun they agree with, decide who acts and who receives, then paraphrase with который. The present and past labels describe stems, not time, and the register contrast written participle versus spoken который clause is the single most useful fact to carry into real reading.

readings.title: Cornell Beginning Russian Grammar — Six deverbal forms
readings.note: Read the whole short page. It states that there are six forms derived from verbs which are not listed separately in a dictionary, names four as participles and two as deverbal adverbs, and prints a chart of the characteristic suffixes: -я/-а and -в(ши) for the adverbs, -щ-ий and -вш-ий for the active participles, -м-ый and -нн-ый/-т-ый for the passive. It also shows the который paraphrase beside each form, which is the reading skill this lesson teaches. The example verbs читать and прочитать are the ones reused in this lesson. Access caveat: this is a legacy 1991 document whose accent glyphs render as unfamiliar characters in some browsers, so read the Cyrillic for its suffixes rather than for its stress marks.

readings.title: Cornell Beginning Russian Grammar — Deverbals: written vs. conversational style
readings.note: One paragraph, and it is the argument of this lesson in miniature: most deverbal forms occur primarily in written Russian, the short forms of past passive participles and the present deverbal adverbs also occur conversationally, and the page ends with the formula 'Written style participles = Conversational style который clauses'. Read it before the longer participle pages, because it tells you why a recognition skill is enough.

readings.title: Cornell Beginning Russian Grammar — Deverbals: Past vs. Present forms
readings.note: Read the paragraph stating that past and present in these forms name the stem they are built from, not their meaning, and then read examples (1) and (2), which print the same participle играющими with a present and a past main verb to show the tense follows the main clause. The page then gives the crucial structural contrast for reading: the subject of a deverbal adverb is the subject of the main clause, while the subject of a participle is the noun it agrees with. That sentence is the difference between the next lesson and this one.

readings.title: Cornell Beginning Russian Grammar — Present active participles
readings.note: Read the first half. It gives the formation rule (-щ- plus adjective endings, built on the non-past stem, so replacing -щ- with -т- yields the 3rd person plural), repeats the который paraphrase, and gives the box-construction example Он рисует играющих во дворе детей, where the participle and its noun bracket the words во дворе. Read as far as the boxed example to see why word order alone cannot be trusted.

readings.title: Cornell Beginning Russian Grammar — Past active participle
readings.note: Read the whole page. It shows -вш- added to the past stem (стоять giving стоявший), states that unlike other participles this one occurs with both imperfective and perfective verbs, and contrasts стоявший with приехавший (pree-YE-khaf-shee — who had arrived). It also notes that participles from -ся verbs never take the variant -сь, which is a useful recognition shortcut. Example sentences here are the ones paraphrased in this lesson.

readings.title: Cornell Beginning Russian Grammar — Deverbal nouns vs. past passive participles
readings.note: Read the whole page for the three diagnostic differences it gives: different endings, but the nouns are all neuter; nouns have -и- after -т- or -н- while participles do not; and the noun has a single -н- where the long participial form has double -нн-. This is the page that turns the opening versus открытый trap from a guess into a check.

readings.title: Wikipedia — Russian grammar, section 'Adjectival participle'
readings.note: Read the opening paragraph and the active present participle subsection. The article states that adjectival participles are active or passive, that imperfective ones can have present or past forms while perfective ones in classical usage can only be past, and that participles are often difficult to distinguish from deverbal adjectives, which matters for some spelling rules. Wikipedia is used here as encyclopaedia-level corroboration of a claim Cornell also makes, not as the primary reference.

visual.title: Collapse a participle into a который clause, then decide active or passive
visual.description: A labelled reading routine for turning any participial phrase into a relative clause you can understand, using agreement and action direction rather than tense guessing.
steps: Find the participle by its adjective ending (-ый, -ая, -ое, -ые or their oblique forms) rather than by looking for a verb with a person ending.
Find the noun it agrees with in gender, number and case; that noun is the head of the phrase.
Decide direction: if the noun performs the action the participle is active (-ущ-/-ющ-/-ащ-/-ящ- present, -вш- past), if it receives the action it is passive (-ем-/-им- present, -нн-/-т- past).
Ignore the present/past label for time; translate the action as simultaneous with the main verb unless a -вш- form tells you it happened earlier.
Replace the participle in your head with который in the same gender and number and in the case the clause needs, then read the sentence.
If a deverbal noun is suspected rather than a participle, check the three diagnostics: neuter noun endings, -и- after -т-/-н-, and a single -н- against the participle's double -нн-.

lessons.title: Gerunds as a reading tool: деепричастия and the 'while -ing' clause
lessons.explanation: The two remaining deverbal forms are the ones Cornell calls deverbal adverbs and other grammars call gerunds. In Russian they are деепричастие (dee-ye-pree-CHA-stee-ye — adverbial participle, gerund), and they are indeclinable, so unlike participles they never change ending for gender, number or case. That makes them easy to spot once you know the two suffix shapes. A present deverbal adverb is built from the non-past stem of an imperfective verb and ends in -я, spelled -а after ч, ш, ш and ж: читая (chee-TA-ya — while reading), говоря (ga-va-RYA — while speaking), лёжа (LYO-zha — while lying). It means 'while doing' and describes action simultaneous with the main verb. A past deverbal adverb is built from the past stem of a perfective verb and ends in -в, with -вши available and obligatory before -сь on reflexive verbs: прочитав (pra-chee-TAF — having read), сказав (ska-ZAF — having said), поженившись (pa-zhe-NEEF-shees — having got married). Cornell prints the pair that makes the contrast visible: Он сидел за столом, читая газету (on see-DYEL za sta-LOM, chee-TA-ya ga-ZYE-too) — He was sitting at the table reading a newspaper, against Прочитав газету, он ушёл (pra-chee-TAF ga-ZYE-too, on oo-SHYOL) — Having read the newspaper, he left. The mechanism that governs both is a single rule and it is the rule that most often breaks a careless reading: the subject of a deverbal adverb is the subject of the main clause. There is no separate subject inside the gerund, so играя in Он говорил с детьми, играя на улице can only mean he was playing, not the children. Spanish speakers have a friendly bridge here, because the Spanish gerundio works the same way grammatically: leyendo el periódico, salió mirrors читая газету, он вышел. But the correspondence is not complete, and the limits matter for reading. Cornell notes that the present deverbal adverb occurs more in written style than in speech, and that some verbs simply have no present deverbal adverb at all, so it is a form to look up rather than derive on demand. It also occurs in fixed expressions you will meet constantly, which is where recognizing it pays off fastest. Whole expressions are also built on gerunds and are met constantly in ordinary prose: честно говоря (CHEST-na ga-va-RYA — frankly speaking) and не говоря уже о Москве are fossilised present deverbal adverbs whose meaning is fixed by convention.
lessons.example: Work through three sentences that use one gerund each, and label the relationship before translating. Simultaneous, imperfective: Читая газету, он ел колбасу (chee-TA-ya ga-ZYE-too, on yel kal-ba-SOO) — While reading the newspaper, he ate sausage. Cornell's own example pairs читая with ел, and the two actions overlap in time. Sequential, perfective: Прочитав газету, он ушёл (pra-chee-TAF ga-ZYE-too, on oo-SHYOL) — Having read the newspaper, he left, where -в tells you the reading finished first. Negative with no separate subject: Он стоял, ничего не говоря (on sta-YAL, nee-chee-VO nye ga-va-RYA) — He stood there without saying anything, which Cornell prints as a typical 'without -ing' use of the present deverbal adverb. Now a reflexive past form: Поженившись, они уехали на запад (pa-zhe-NEEF-shees, a-NEE oo-YE-kha-lee na ZA-pad) — Having got married, they went west, where -вшись sits at the end of the form. Read each sentence twice: once as written, and once with the gerund expanded into a full clause joined by и or когда, for instance Он стоял и ничего не говорил. If the expansion produces a sentence with the same subject, you have read the gerund correctly; if it produces two different subjects, you have misassigned it.
lessons.question: In Он говорил с детьми, играя на улице, who was playing in the street, and which single rule decides it?
lessons.answer: He was playing. The rule is that the subject of a deverbal adverb is the subject of the main clause, so playing in the street can only refer back to the subject of говорил.
lessons.distractor: The children were playing, because играя agrees with детьми in the same way a participle would.
lessons.correction: Играя is a deverbal adverb, not a participle, and that distinction is exactly the point. Cornell contrasts the two side by side: with a deverbal adverb — Он говорил с детьми, играя на улице — the one playing is the subject of the main clause, while with a participle — Он говорил с детьми, играющими на улице — the one playing is the noun the participle agrees with, namely the children. Gerunds are indeclinable and never agree with anything, so they cannot attach to детьми. If you want the children to be playing, you need the participle играющими or a который clause, not играя.

depth.definitions: A deverbal adverb, or gerund, is an indeclinable verb form that functions like an adverb inside a sentence. Present deverbal adverbs are formed from the non-past stem of imperfective verbs with -я/-а and mean 'while doing'; past deverbal adverbs are formed from the past stem of perfective verbs with -в (or -вши, obligatory before -сь) and mean 'having done'. Simultaneous means the two actions overlap in time; sequential means one finishes before the other begins. Indeclinable means the form has one shape only and never changes for case, gender or number.
depth.mechanism: The design of the gerund solves a compression problem in a different way from the participle. A participle attaches to a noun and builds a reduced relative clause; a gerund attaches to the whole sentence and builds a reduced adverbial clause of time, manner or cause. Because it is indeclinable, it carries no agreement information at all, so all of its meaning comes from the verb stem it was built on and from the subject it shares. Cornell drives the consequence home with the minimal pair играющими against играя, and Wikipedia's adverbial participle section states the same design: these forms express an earlier or simultaneous action providing context for the sentence, they are not declined, they inherit the aspect of their verb, and imperfective ones are usually present while perfective ones can only be past. Two reading limits follow. First, a gerund with no visible subject must be tied to the main clause subject, so when the Russian means two different actors the language must switch to a full clause with и, а or a который construction. Second, not every verb has a gerund: Cornell says some verbs have no present deverbal adverb and tells the reader to check a dictionary, so encountering a missing form is a lexical fact, not a gap in your understanding. A rare passive gerund also exists for the verb быть, namely будучи (BOO-doo-chee — being), which Wikipedia's adverbial-participle section records as usable with either an instrumental participle or a nominative short adjective.
depth.secondExample: Set a gerund against the three other ways Russian expresses the same sequence, exactly as Cornell's time-clause page lays them out. Joined by and: Он пообедал и ушёл (on pa-a-BYE-dal ee oo-SHYOL) — He ate dinner and left. Time clause with a correlative: После того как он пообедал, он ушёл (PO-slye ta-VO kak on pa-a-BYE-dal, on oo-SHYOL) — After he ate dinner, he left. Preposition plus noun: После обеда он ушёл (PO-slye a-BYE-da on oo-SHYOL) — He left after dinner. Reduced gerund clause: Пообедав, он ушёл (pa-a-BYE-daf, on oo-SHYOL) — Having eaten dinner, he left. All four mean the same sequence, and Cornell's point on that page is that Russian clauses must be introduced by clause introducers rather than by prepositions, which is why the third form cannot take a clause and the gerund exists. Read the four in order and notice that only the gerund and the time clause tell you explicitly which action came first.
depth.mistake: Three errors recur. The first attaches the gerund to the wrong noun, as in reading играя as referring to детьми. The second reads a gerund as a finite verb and then looks for a second subject, producing a sentence with two subjects and no main verb. The third treats the gerund as a tense marker, so that читая is translated 'read' in past time rather than 'while reading'. Diagnose by a single question: what is the subject of the main clause? Assign every gerund to that subject, then decide from the aspect whether the two actions overlap (imperfective, simultaneous) or are sequential (perfective, prior).
depth.application: Nonblocking task: find four gerunds in a short news paragraph or in any text you already have, and for each one write the full clause it replaces, joined with и, когда or после того как. Model response for one line: Прочитав письмо, она позвонила (pra-chee-TAF pees-MO, a-NA paz-va-NEE-la) — Having read the letter, she phoned, which expands to Она прочитала письмо и позвонила, and Она позвонила после того, как прочитала письмо. Self-review rubric: (1) the same subject appears in both clauses; (2) the aspect of the gerund matches simultaneous or sequential meaning; (3) the expanded sentence is grammatical Russian; (4) I did not translate the gerund as a finite past verb. The task is nonblocking and no audio or recording is required.
depth.summary: Gerunds are compressed adverbial clauses. They are indeclinable, so they carry no agreement, and they borrow their subject from the main clause — which is why the single most valuable reading habit is to name the main subject before assigning the action. Present forms built on imperfective stems signal overlap; past forms built on perfective stems signal prior completion. Like participles, they belong mostly to written style, and Spanish speakers already know the shape of the idea from the gerundio.

visual.title: Assign every gerund to the main clause subject
visual.description: A labelled routine for reading a Russian gerund by finding the main subject first, then deciding simultaneous or sequential action from the aspect of the form.
steps: Locate the main clause and name its subject explicitly; this is quiet work that decides everything else in the sentence.
Identify the gerund by its shape: -я/-а on a non-past stem (present, imperfective) or -в/-вши/-шись on a past stem (past, perfective).
Confirm the gerund has no agreeing adjective ending; if it does agree with a noun, you are looking at a participle, not a gerund.
Attach the gerund's action to the main clause subject, never to another noun in the sentence, and say so aloud before translating.
Decide time relationship from the form: present deverbal adverb means the two actions overlap, past deverbal adverb means the action finished first.

lessons.title: Relative clauses with который: the joining word that carries two agreements at once
lessons.explanation: A relative clause adds information about a noun without starting a new sentence, and Russian builds almost all of them with one word: который (ka-TO-ryy — who, which, that). The word looks like an ordinary adjective and behaves like one, which is what makes it both powerful and easy to get wrong. Cornell states the governing rule in a single sentence: который agrees with its antecedent in gender and number, but its case depends on its function in its own clause. That is two separate agreements in one word, and they can point in different directions. Its gender and number come from the noun it refers back to; its case comes from the job it does inside the relative clause — subject, object, possessor, or the object of a preposition. Cornell's own examples make the split visible. Дайте мне книгу, которая лежит на столе (DAY-tye mnye KNEE-goo, ka-TO-ra-ya lee-ZHEET na sta-LYE) — Give me the book which is lying on the table, where которая is feminine singular to match книга and nominative because it is the subject of лежит. Change the noun to a masculine one and only the gender shifts: Дайте мне нож, который лежит на столе (nosh, ka-TO-ryy). Now make the relative word an object, and the case follows the clause rather than the antecedent: книга, которую мы читаем (KNEE-ga, ka-TO-roo-yoo my chee-TA-yem) — the book which we are reading, accusative feminine because it is the object of читаем. Cornell's extended example shows the case moving to genitive after a preposition in the other clause: Вы разговаривали с другим Петром Ильичом, у которого нет жены (vy raz-ga-VA-ree-va-lee s droo-GEEM Pyet-ROM Eel-YEE-chom, oo ka-TO-ra-va nyet zhe-NY) — You were talking with another Pyotr Ilyich, who doesn't have a wife. The signal to watch is the comma: the relative clause is set off, and everything after который belongs to that second clause. Russian also uses что and кто as joining words, but который is the workhorse for things and people alike, and it is the one whose agreement pattern rewards deliberate practice.
lessons.example: Build one relative clause in four steps and watch each ending do its own job. Step one, choose the antecedent: я знаю женщину (ya ZNA-yoo ZHEN-shee-noo) — I know the woman, accusative feminine. Step two, decide the relative word's function in its own clause. If she is the one who works there, the relative word is the subject and takes nominative: я знаю женщину, которая работает здесь (ka-TO-ra-ya ra-BO-ta-yet zdyes) — I know the woman who works here. If she is the one I see, the relative word is the object and takes accusative: я знаю женщину, которую я вижу каждый день (ka-TO-roo-yoo ya VEE-zhoo KAZH-dyy dyen) — I know the woman whom I see every day. Step three, add a preposition when the verb needs one, and put it immediately before the relative word: дом, в котором мы живём (dom, v ka-TO-rom my zhee-VYOM) — the house in which we live, where в governs the prepositional case and the gender and number still come from дом. Step four, move the clause if the sentence becomes clumsy: Cornell's box-construction page shows that written Russian can place the relative or participial material before the noun, giving constructions whose word order is impossible to translate literally without reordering. Read the four versions aloud and, for each, say the antecedent's gender and number first, then the relative word's case — never the other way round.
lessons.question: In дом, в котором мы живём, why is котором masculine singular prepositional, and which part of the word comes from which agreement?
lessons.answer: Masculine singular comes from the antecedent дом; the prepositional case comes from its function inside the second clause, where the preposition в governs the prepositional case and мы живём needs a location phrase.
lessons.distractor: Masculine singular comes from мы, and the prepositional case comes from дом, because a relative word copies the case of the noun it follows.
lessons.correction: A relative word never copies the case of its antecedent. Cornell states the rule directly for этот word: который agrees with its antecedent in gender and number, but its case depends on its function in its own clause. Дом supplies masculine singular, which rules out которая and которое; the clause в котором мы живём supplies the prepositional case, because в as a location preposition governs the prepositional, exactly as it does in в доме. If you swapped the logic and let the antecedent supply the case, you would produce в который мы живём, which is ungrammatical because the preposition's government has not been satisfied.

depth.definitions: An antecedent is the noun a relative clause describes. A relative clause is a clause that modifies a noun and cannot stand alone. Agreement in gender and number means the relative word carries the same gender and number as its antecedent; case assignment means the relative word takes whatever case its function inside its own clause requires, including after a preposition. Box construction is Cornell's term for a noun phrase in which an adjective plus its dependent material bracket the noun.
depth.mechanism: The reason который looks confusing is that it is doing two jobs with one set of endings, and the two jobs are decided by different parts of the sentence. Gender and number are inherited from outside the clause; case is decided inside it. Cornell's example set deliberately varies only one variable at a time — книга with которая and нож with который isolates gender, while книга with которая and книга with которую isolates case — which is exactly how a learner should practise. Wikipedia's subordination section adds a design fact that explains why relative clauses are less frequent in Russian than in English: the article states that Russian has fewer subordinate clauses than English because participles and adverbial participles often take the place of a relative pronoun and verb combination, and it gives человек, потерявший надежду for 'a man who has lost all hope'. So the same content can appear as a который clause in speech or as a participle in writing, and lessons 71 and 73 are two routes to one meaning. Two limits are worth stating. First, Russian normally places the relative clause immediately after the antecedent, so a long string of nouns before the clause can make the reference ambiguous. Second, который is not the only joining word: кто and что also introduce clauses, but который covers people and things without the case quirks of кто. The written forms the same content takes are also common inside the noun phrase: покрытая снегом улица (pa-KRY-ta-ya SNYE-gom OO-lee-tsa — the street covered with snow) and играющих во дворе детей (ee-GRA-yoo-shcheekh va dvar-YE dye-TYEY — the children playing in the courtyard) are box constructions in which the participle and the words depending on it bracket the noun, so the ending on the left-hand word matches the noun rather than the words in between.
depth.secondExample: Compare a который clause with its participial twin, because the meaning is identical and only the register differs. Spoken: Он подошёл к милиционеру, который стоял у двери (on pa-da-SHYOL k mee-lee-tsa-NYE-roo, ka-TO-ryy sta-YAL oo DVYE-ree) — He approached the policeman who was standing by the door. Written, with a participle: Он подошёл к милиционеру, стоявшему у двери (sta-YAV-she-moo oo DVYE-ree), where стоявшему is masculine singular dative to match милиционеру and its case, like который's, comes from the main clause verb подошёл, which governs the dative. Now reorder into a box construction: Он подошёл к стоявшему у двери милиционеру, where the words у двери have been pulled inside the noun phrase. Cornell prints all three as equivalent. Notice that the ending on стоявшему and the ending on которому would be the same — the two designs assign case identically, and that is why one can be paraphrased as the other.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first takes the case of the relative word from the antecedent instead of from its own clause, producing в который мы живём for в котором. The second takes gender and number from the wrong noun, which happens when the sentence contains two nouns of different genders and the clause is far from its antecedent. The third omits the comma, hiding the boundary between the main clause and the relative clause. The fourth confuses который with кто and produces a clause that has no antecedent to agree with. Diagnose in a fixed order every time: underline the antecedent, write its gender and number above который, then ask what role который plays in the clause immediately following it, and only then choose the ending.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: write six relative clauses about work or study, two where который is the subject, two where it is the object, and two where a preposition governs it. Model response for one line: Я работаю в офисе, который находится в центре (ya ra-BO-ta-yoo v a-FEE-sye, ka-TO-ryy na-KHO-deet-sya v TSYEN-trye) — I work in an office which is in the centre. Self-review rubric: (1) the relative word's gender and number match the underlined antecedent; (2) its case matches its own function, including the case a preposition requires; (3) the clause sits immediately after the antecedent; (4) I could also express the same content as a participle and can say which version is written style. The task is nonblocking.
depth.summary: Который carries inherited gender and number from its antecedent and its own case from its clause, so reading a relative clause means naming the antecedent first and the clause role second. The comma marks the boundary, prepositions sit directly before the relative word, and the same content can be repackaged as a participle when the register is written. Get the order of decisions right and the endings stop being a memory problem.

lessons.title: Cause, purpose, and concession: потому что, чтобы, and хотя
lessons.explanation: Once you can build a relative clause, the next step in real Russian is joining clauses by meaning rather than by position. Three relationships carry most of the work: cause, purpose, and concession. Russian marks cause with two common introducers, and they are not interchangeable. Потому что (pa-ta-MOO shta — because) gives the reason for an already stated fact and is the ordinary spoken choice; так как (tak kak — since, for the reason that) is bookish and often opens a sentence, presenting the reason as known background. The result can be flagged forward with поэтому (pa-EH-ta-moo — therefore, that is why), which behaves like a connector rather than a subordinator. Wikipedia's subordination section lists потому что and так как among the complementizers that introduce subordinate clauses and glosses так как as meaning 'for the reason that', which is precisely the distinction between reporting a cause and presupposing one. Purpose works with a single introducer, чтобы (SHTO-by — so that, in order to), but it has two shapes and choosing between them is the main skill of this lesson. With an infinitive, чтобы means 'in order to' and both verbs share one subject: Я купил учебник, чтобы заниматься русским языком (ya koo-PEEL oo-CHEB-neek, SHTO-by za-nee-MAT-sya ROOS-keem yee-zy-KOM) — I bought a textbook in order to study Russian. With a past-tense form, чтобы introduces a full clause and signals that the two verbs have different subjects: Я хотел, чтобы она встала (ya kha-TYEL, SHTO-by a-NA VSTA-la) — I wanted her to get up. Cornell warns about this explicitly, because English uses an infinitive in both situations and a literal translation will mislead you. Concession is marked by хотя (kha-TYA — although) or, in a heavier register, несмотря на (nee-smat-RYA na — despite, followed by the accusative). Finally, one structural fact ties cause, purpose and concession together: Russian clauses must be introduced by clause introducers, not by prepositions, so a prepositional phrase cannot simply be given a subject and a verb. That is why Russian says после обеда but после того как он пообедал. The purpose question itself has a dedicated word, as in Зачем тебе карандаш? (za-CHEM tye-BYE ka-ran-DASH — What do you need a pencil for?), and the answer is a чтобы plus infinitive phrase rather than a full clause.
lessons.example: Take one content idea and express it as cause, purpose and concession, changing only the introducer and the structure. Cause with потому что: Я остался дома, потому что была плохая погода (ya as-TA-lya-sya DO-ma, pa-ta-MOO shta by-LA PLA-kha-ya pa-GO-da) — I stayed at home because the weather was bad. The same content as background with так как: Так как погода была плохая, я остался дома (tak kak pa-GO-da by-LA PLA-kha-ya, ya as-TA-lya-sya DO-ma). Result with поэтому: Погода была плохая, поэтому я остался дома (pa-EH-ta-moo ya as-TA-lya-sya DO-ma). Now purpose. Same subject, infinitive: Я вернулся, чтобы закрыть окно (ya ver-NUL-sya, SHTO-by zak-RYT ak-NO) — I came back in order to close the window. Different subjects, past form: Я хотел, чтобы ты закрыл окно (ya kha-TYEL, SHTO-by ty zak-RYL ak-NO) — I wanted you to close the window. Notice that ты is nominative and the verb is past, which Cornell records as the construction required when the two subjects differ. Now concession: Хотя погода была плохая, я вышел погулять (kha-TYA pa-GO-da by-LA PLA-kha-ya, ya VY-shel pa-goo-LYAT) — Although the weather was bad, I went out for a walk. Read all six and label each aloud as cause, background cause, result, purpose with one subject, purpose with two subjects, or concession. The label comes before the form.
lessons.question: You want to say 'I want him to study Russian'. Why is Я хочу, чтобы он занимался русским языком correct, and why is Я хочу заниматься русским языком wrong?
lessons.answer: Because the two verbs have different subjects — I want, he studies — so Russian requires чтобы plus a past-tense form after a full clause, with the second subject in the nominative; the infinitive is reserved for sentences where one subject does both actions.
lessons.distractor: Because заниматься is imperfective and the rule requires a perfective verb after хотеть whenever a second subject appears.
lessons.correction: Aspect is not what decides this. Cornell's page on чтобы with wishes, commands and advice gives the contrast directly: Я хочу петь means I want to sing, where one person does both, while Я хочу, чтобы он пел means I want him to sing, where the subjects differ, and the page warns that learners are misled by the English infinitive in 'I want him to sing'. The same page adds the meaning-changing pair Он сказала, что они подписали письмо — 'she said that they had signed the letter' — against Она сказала, чтобы они подписали письмо — 'she told them to sign the letter'. So the rule to apply is about subjects and about whether the clause reports a fact or asks for an action, not about aspect at all.

depth.definitions: Cause answers why something happened; purpose answers what the action was intended to achieve; concession grants a fact that would normally prevent the outcome and states that the outcome happened anyway. A complementizer is a word that introduces a subordinate clause and removes its ability to stand alone. An infinitive is the dictionary form of a verb, ending in -ть or -ти, which carries no person or tense. The accusative is the case Russian uses both for direct objects and, after certain prepositions such as несмотря на, for the object of a preposition.
depth.mechanism: Each of the three relations is signalled by a different part of the sentence, and that is why they are worth learning together. Cause places the reason after the effect with потому что, or before it with так как or поэтому, and the choice is largely a matter of register and of whether the reason is presented as new information or as shared background. Purpose is decided by subject identity: if one subject performs both verbs, чтобы takes an infinitive; if the wanting and the doing belong to different people, чтобы needs a past-tense form in a full clause. Cornell's rule is stated twice in the grammar review, once as the chtoby-with-wishes page and once as the chtoby-cannot-take-an-infinitive page, and the second page notes that some verbs such as попросить allow both constructions while others such as хотеть and сказать allow only the clause. Concession sits outside both patterns and is largely lexical: хотя introduces a clause, while несмотря на introduces a noun phrase in the accusative. One structural limit applies to all three: Russian does not let a preposition introduce a clause, which is why the language has the correlative после того как where English can use a bare preposition. Wikipedia's coordination section adds the related fact that Russian conjunctions come in conjoining, oppositional and separative families, with но, однако and зато available when the concession is strong enough to feel like contrast.
depth.secondExample: Contrast purpose expressed as a clause with purpose expressed as a prepositional phrase, because the two are easy to confuse when reading quickly. Clause with чтобы: Я приехал, чтобы увидеть тебя (ya pree-YE-khal, SHTO-by oo-VEE-dyet tye-BYA) — I came in order to see you. Prepositional phrase with для: Я купил это для тебя (ya koo-PEEL EH-ta dlya tye-BYA) — I bought this for you, where для takes the genitive and, as Cornell's page states, always emphasizes good intentions. Cornell's example set makes the difference concrete: Я тебе купила роман — I bought you a novel, uses the bare dative, while Я этот роман купила специально для тебя — I bought this novel specially for you, needs для because the adverb специально makes the benefactive meaning explicit. Now read a concession beside its contrastive cousin: Хотя он устал, он работал is 'although he was tired, he worked', while Он устал, но работал is 'he was tired, but he worked'. Both are correct; the first subordinates one clause to the other, the second leaves them equal in weight.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first uses an infinitive after чтобы when the two clauses have different subjects, producing Я хочу заниматься when the meaning is actually about someone else. The second uses чтобы where a fact is being reported, which changes meaning: сказать, что reports, сказать, чтобы instructs. The third uses потому что for a reason the listener already knows, where так как or a потому что late in the clause would fit the register better. The fourth inserts a preposition before a clause, producing something like после обеда когда rather than после того как. Diagnose by naming the relation first, then the subject pattern: cause means check whether the reason is new or shared; purpose means check whether one subject or two; concession means check whether a clause or a noun phrase follows.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: write a six-sentence mini-report about a decision you made at work or in study, using one потому что, one так как or поэтому, two чтобы clauses with different subject patterns, and one хотя. Model response for one line: Я не пошёл на встречу, потому что заболел, хотя уже купил билет (ya nye pash-YOL na VSTRYE-choo, pa-ta-MOO shta za-ba-LYEL, kha-TYA oo-ZHE koo-PEEL bee-LYET) — I did not go to the meeting because I was ill, although I had already bought a ticket. Self-review rubric: (1) each introducer matches the relation I intended; (2) after чтобы, the verb form matches whether the subjects are the same; (3) no preposition introduces a clause; (4) the aspect of each verb matches whether the event is bounded or habitual. The task is nonblocking.
depth.summary: Cause, purpose and concession are three ways of joining clauses by meaning. Потому что reports a reason, так как presupposes one, поэтому announces a result; чтобы takes an infinitive for one subject and a past-tense clause for two; хотя introduces a concession as a clause while несмотря на takes a noun phrase. The unifying constraint is that Russian clauses are opened by clause introducers rather than prepositions, which is why correlatives such as после того как exist at all.

visual.description: A labelled decision sequence for cause, purpose and concession that fixes both the joining word and the verb form before the sentence is spoken.
steps: Name the relation you want: reason for a fact, intended goal, or an admitted fact that did not prevent the outcome.
For a reason, decide whether the listener already knows it; if yes consider так как or поэтому, if it is new information use потому что.
For a goal, ask how many subjects are involved: one subject takes чтобы plus an infinitive, two subjects take чтобы plus a nominative second subject and a past-tense verb.
For a benefit expressed as a noun rather than a clause, use для plus the genitive and reserve it for cases where the good intention is the point.
For a concession, use хотя plus a full clause when the material is a clause, and несмотря на plus the accusative when it is a noun phrase.
Check that no preposition is standing in front of a clause, and label the finished sentence aloud by relation before translating it.

lessons.title: Time expressions and sequencing: choosing the case before choosing the words
lessons.explanation: Time in Russian is expressed by case and preposition working together, and the case, not the English word, is what decides the meaning. Cornell's summary page reduces the system to a table organised by the kind of time noun you have. Saying something happened on a certain day uses в plus the accusative: в среду (v SREE-doo — on Wednesday). Saying it happened in a month or a season uses в plus the prepositional: в январе (v yan-va-RYE — in January), в прошлом году (v PROSH-lam ga-DOO — last year). Times of day and the seasons work without any preposition at all, taking the instrumental: утром (OOT-ram — in the morning), вечером (VYE-chee-ram — in the evening), весной (vyes-NOY — in spring), летом (LYE-tam — in summer). Dates take the genitive with no preposition: пятого мая (PYA-ta-va MA-ya — on the fifth of May). Duration is different again, and this is where English speakers slip: an action lasting a week takes the accusative with no preposition, я был там неделю (ya byl tam nee-DYE-lyoo — I was there for a week), while the same accusative with тому назад (ta-MOO na-ZAD — ago) places the point in the past: неделю тому назад (a week ago). Cornell notes that тому is optional in that expression. A point in the future or a later moment takes через plus the accusative: через неделю (CHYE-ryez nee-DYE-lyoo — in a week, or a week later). Frequency has its own two patterns: по plus the dative plural for habitual repetition, по утрам (pa OOT-ram — every morning), and каждый plus the accusative for the same idea, каждую неделю (KAZH-doo-yoo nee-DYE-lyoo — every week). A rate is counted with раз plus в plus the accusative: два раза в день (dva RA-za v dyen — twice a day). Spanish speakers have partial help here, because hace una semana matches неделю тому назад and dentro de una semana matches через неделю, but Spanish generally uses a preposition where Russian may use none. Finally, sequencing between clauses is done with correlatives rather than prepositions: после того как (PO-slye ta-VO kak — after), до того как (da ta-VO kak — before), в то время как (v ta VRYE-mya kak — while), and с ... до ... (s ... da ...) for a span from one point to another. One clarification about conjunction choice: потому что (pa-ta-MOO shta — because) and a time correlative such as после того как occupy the same grammatical slot, since both open a subordinate clause, but only the first one expresses a cause.
lessons.example: Read one week as a story and watch the case change with the meaning. Monday: В понедельник я был в офисе (v pa-nee-DYEL-neek ya byl v A-fee-sye) — On Monday I was at the office, в plus accusative for a named day. Morning detail: Утром я пил кофе (OOT-ram ya peel KO-fye) — In the morning I drank coffee, bare instrumental for a part of the day. Habit: По утрам я всегда пью кофе (pa OOT-ram ya vsyeg-DA pyoo KO-fye) — Mornings I always drink coffee, по plus dative plural for habit, which Cornell prints as пью кофе по утрам. Duration: В среду я работал шесть часов (v SREE-doo ya ra-BO-tal shest cha-SOV) — On Wednesday I worked six hours, accusative for a measured span. Span: Я был в отпуске с понедельника до среды (ya byl v OT-poos-kye s pa-nee-DYEL-nee-ka da sree-DY) — I was on holiday from Monday to Wednesday, с and до plus genitive for the two endpoints. Later moment: Я вернусь через два дня (ya ver-NOOS CHYE-ryez dva DNYA) — I will come back in two days, через plus accusative for the interval ahead. Ago: Я приехал неделю тому назад (ya pree-YE-khal nee-DYE-lyoo ta-MOO na-ZAD) — I arrived a week ago. Now a sequencing clause: После того как я закончил работу, я пошёл домой (PO-slye ta-VO kak ya za-KON-cheel ra-BO-too, ya pa-SHYOL da-MOY) — After I finished work, I went home. Read the eight sentences and, for each, name the case of the time word aloud before translating, because the case is the meaning.
lessons.question: How do you say 'in a week' versus 'a week ago', and what exactly changes between the two expressions?
lessons.answer: 'In a week' is через неделю, with через plus the accusative pointing forward; 'a week ago' is неделю тому назад, with the bare accusative plus тому назад pointing back, or simply неделю назад since тому is optional.
lessons.distractor: Both are неделю, because the accusative of a time noun always means a week in the past and only the verb tense distinguishes them.
lessons.correction: The accusative alone is neutral about direction: it measures a span, as in я был там неделю, 'I spent a week there'. Direction comes from the extra words, not from the case. Cornell's elapsed-time page pairs Я это сделаю через неделю, 'I'll do it in a week', with Он приехал через неделю, 'He came a week later', showing that через always points forward from a reference point, while the ago page gives Она ездила туда неделю тому назад for 'she went there a week ago' and notes that тому is optional. Spanish makes the same contrast with dentro de una semana against hace una semana, so the distinction is not exotic; it is the case plus particle that does the work in Russian.

depth.definitions: A time expression is a phrase that locates an event in time or measures how long it lasts. Duration is how long something lasts; a point in time is when something happens; frequency is how often it happens. A correlative is a fixed pair such as то, как in после того как, in which the first part is inflected by the governing preposition and the second part is fixed. Case government means that a preposition requires a particular case of the noun that follows it.
depth.mechanism: The system looks arbitrary only until you see that each English preposition has been split into a case plus a preposition that match the kind of time noun involved. Cornell's summary page lays out the split explicitly, and its wording is worth keeping: the preposition and case you use to state the time when something occurs depends on the noun, so saying that something happened on a certain day differs from saying it happened in a certain month or season. Days of the week take в plus accusative; months take в plus prepositional; parts of the day and the four seasons take the bare instrumental, which is the only place where no preposition appears at all; dates take the bare genitive. Duration, elapsed time and frequency add a second layer of machinery: the bare accusative measures, тому назад reaches back, через reaches forward, по plus dative plural and каждый plus accusative both express habit but with different emphasis, and раз plus в plus accusative counts a rate. Cornell's page on time clauses explains why Russian needs correlatives at all, namely that a clause in Russian must be introduced by a clause introducer and cannot be introduced by a preposition, so после обед becomes after dinner while после того как он пообедал introduces a clause. The page on с ... до ... adds that the second endpoint can be made inclusive with по plus the accusative instead of до plus the genitive, which is the difference between 'from Monday to Wednesday' and 'from Monday through Wednesday'.
depth.secondExample: Contrast two time phrases that differ only in the preposition and therefore in the case. Saying when: В среду у меня встреча (v SREE-doo oo mee-NYA FSTRYE-cha) — On Wednesday I have a meeting, в plus accusative for a day. Saying for how long: Я буду в Москве неделю (ya BOO-doo v Mask-VYE nee-DYE-lyoo) — I will be in Moscow for a week, bare accusative for duration, with no preposition at all. Now add the endpoints: Я буду в Москве с пятницы по воскресенье (ya BOO-doo v Mask-VYE s PYAT-nee-tsy pa vas-kree-SYE-nye) — I will be in Moscow from Friday through Sunday, where с takes the genitive and по takes the accusative, compared with the non-inclusive с пятницы до воскресенья. Cornell prints the pair я там была с понедельника до среды against я там была с понедельника по среду and states that по makes the second point included. Finally set a frequency pair side by side: Я езжу туда по средам (ya YE-zhgoo too-DA pa srye-DAM) — I go there on Wednesdays, and Я езжу туда каждую среду — I go there every Wednesday. Both are habitual; по plus dative plural groups the habit into a schedule, while каждый plus accusative treats each week separately.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first transfers an English preposition into Russian, producing something like на утре instead of the bare утром. The second confuses when with how long, so that неделю is used for 'in a week' rather than for the length of a stay. The third uses в plus prepositional for days of the week, producing в среде instead of в среду. The fourth builds clause-level sequences with a bare preposition, producing после обеда as though it could carry a verb phrase. Diagnose by asking which question the phrase answers: when, how long, how often, or in what sequence. The question fixes the case, and only then is the vocabulary chosen.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: write a diary entry of eight sentences covering one day and one week, using at least one example each of when, duration, a later moment, an elapsed span, a frequency and a sequencing clause. Model response for two lines: Обычно по утрам я работаю дома, но в среду я был в офисе с девяти до шести; через неделю я вернусь туда на два дня (a-BYCH-na pa OOT-ram ya ra-BO-ta-yoo DO-ma, no v SREE-doo ya byl v A-fee-sye s dee-vee-TEE da shes-TEE; CHYE-ryez nee-DYE-lyoo ya ver-NOOS too-DA na dva DNYA). Self-review rubric: (1) each phrase answers the question I intended; (2) days take в plus accusative and months take в plus prepositional; (3) parts of the day and seasons take the bare instrumental; (4) sequence clauses use a correlative rather than a bare preposition. The task is nonblocking.
depth.summary: Russian time expressions are decided by case before vocabulary. Days take в plus accusative, months в plus prepositional, parts of day and seasons the bare instrumental, dates the bare genitive. Duration is a bare accusative, ago adds тому назад, a future point adds через, habit divides between по plus dative plural and каждый plus accusative, and sequence is carried by correlatives because a Russian clause cannot be opened by a preposition.

visual.title: Ask the time question first, then choose the case and preposition
visual.description: A labelled decision sequence that turns an English time phrase into the correct Russian case and preposition by identifying the type of time first.
steps: Ask which question the phrase answers: when, how long, how often, or in what sequence.
For when on a named day, use в plus the accusative; for a month or a year, use в plus the prepositional.
For when at a part of the day or in a season, use the bare instrumental with no preposition.
For a date, use the bare genitive; for how long, use the bare accusative.
For a point in the future or an interval later, use через plus the accusative; for a point in the past, use the accusative plus тому назад, or давно for a vague past.
For habit, choose по plus the dative plural for a schedule or каждый plus the accusative for individual occurrences; for a rate, use раз plus в plus the accusative.
For sequence between clauses, use a correlative such as после того как or до того как, never a bare preposition.

questions.prompt: A paragraph reads: Книга, читаемая нами, интересная. Which reading is correct, and which ending decided it?
questions.answer: 'The book which we are reading is interesting': читаемая is a present passive participle agreeing with книга, so the book receives the reading, and the -ем- suffix comes from the non-past мы-form читаем plus the adjective ending.
questions.distractor: 'The book read us': читаемая is an active participle, so книга performs the action of читать on us.
questions.correction: The -ем- suffix belongs to the present passive participle, which Cornell builds directly on the non-past мы-form читаем and shows is formed from imperfective verbs, so its meaning is on-going action received by the noun. Active would require -ущ-/-ющ- or -ащ-/-ящ-. The feminine ending -ая shows agreement with книга in gender, number and case, which rules out a finite verb reading entirely.

questions.prompt: You meet Он говорил с детьми, играя на улице and want to know who was playing. What rule settles it, and how would you rewrite the sentence to make the children the players?
questions.answer: The subject of a deverbal adverb is the subject of the main clause, so he was playing; to make the children the players, use the participle играющими or the clause которые играли.
questions.distractor: Играя agrees with детьми, so the children were playing; to make him the player you would add a second subject.
questions.correction: Gerunds are indeclinable and carry no agreement at all, which is why they cannot attach to детьми. Cornell prints the minimal pair Он говорил с детьми, играющими на улице against Он говорил с детьми, играя на улице and states that the participle's subject is the noun it agrees with while the deverbal adverb's subject is the main clause subject. So only the participial or a который form can assign the playing to the children.

questions.prompt: In Вы разговаривали с другим Петром Ильичом, у которого нет жены, why is которого genitive rather than dative to match Петром Ильичом?
questions.answer: Because который inherits only gender and number from its antecedent, while its case comes from its own clause, where the preposition у governs the genitive.
questions.distractor: Because который always takes the genitive after the verb разговаривать, regardless of the preposition.
questions.correction: Cornell states the rule in one sentence on the kotoryj page: the word agrees with its antecedent in gender and number, but its case depends on its function in its own clause. Here the function is the object of у, and у requires the genitive, so которого is correct. Notice that masculine singular does come from Пётр, which is why the form is not которой.

questions.prompt: You want to say 'I want him to study Russian'. Which construction is required, and what specifically would go wrong if you used an infinitive?
questions.answer: Я хочу, чтобы он занимался русским языком: two different subjects require чтобы with a nominative second subject and a past-tense verb; an infinitive would claim that one person both wants and studies.
questions.distractor: Я хочу заниматься русским языком is correct, because хотеть always takes an infinitive and the second subject stands in the dative.
questions.correction: Cornell's chtoby-with-wishes page warns that learners are misled by the English infinitive in 'I want him to sing' and states that if the two verbs have different subjects you must use чтобы plus an л-form. The infinitive construction Я хочу петь means 'I want to sing', where one subject does both. Aspect is not the variable here; subject identity is.

questions.prompt: A learner writes Я приеду в неделю for 'I will come in a week'. What is wrong, and what should replace it?
questions.answer: В plus the accusative marks a named day or clock time, not a forward interval; the correct form is через неделю, which points forward from now.
questions.distractor: In is correct because в plus the accusative always means a period of time in the future, so only the noun needs to change to неделю.
questions.correction: Cornell's elapsed-time page pairs Я это сделаю через неделю with Он приехал через неделю to show that через plus the accusative measures an interval forward from a reference point, while в plus the accusative locates an event on a named day, as in в среду. The bare accusative неделю would mean duration, 'for a week', without any preposition. Three different meanings sit behind three different shapes, and 'in a week' belongs to через.

units.title: Hearing and speaking: reported speech, register, idiom, and long narration

lessons.title: Reported speech and hearsay: что, ли, and what Russian does not do to tense
lessons.explanation: Reporting what someone said is a reading and listening skill before it is a speaking skill, because Russian reports differently from English in two ways that are easy to miss. The first difference is tense. Wikipedia's indirect-speech article states the rule in one line for Russian: indirect speech uses the same verb tense as the equivalent sentence in direct speech, and it prints the pair Я не люблю шоколад — 'I don't like chocolate' — beside Она сказала, что не любит шоколад (a-NA ska-ZA-la, shta nye LYO-beet sha-ka-LAT) — 'She said that she didn't like chocolate', literally 'she said that she doesn't like chocolate'. English would backshift the tense; Russian does not. The reported verb keeps the shape it had in the original utterance, so a present-tense verb stays present inside a past-tense report. The second difference is the joining word, and here Russian splits three ways. A reported statement is introduced by что (shta — that): Он сказал, что он работает в банке (on ska-ZAL, shta on ra-BO-ta-yet v BAN-kye) — He said that he works in a bank. A reported command, request or wish is introduced by чтобы with a past-tense form instead, and this is not a tense change but a different construction: Она сказала, чтобы они подписали письмо (a-NA ska-ZA-la, SHTO-by a-NEE pad-pee-SA-lee pees-MO) — She told them to sign the letter, against Она сказала, что они подписали письмо — She said that they had signed the letter. A reported yes-or-no question is introduced by the unstressed particle ли (lee — whether), which comes immediately after the word being questioned: Вы не скажете, будет ли сегодня собрание? (vy nye SKA-zhe-tye, BOO-dyet lee see-VOD-nya sab-RA-nee-ye) — Could you tell me whether there is a meeting today? Cornell notes that ли is used mostly in indirect questions and corresponds to English 'whether' or colloquial 'if', and adds a warning that matters: если is not the Russian for 'whether', because если is reserved for real conditions. Reported wh-questions need no particle at all, since the question word itself does the joining: Я спросил, где он живёт (ya spra-SEEL, gdye on zhee-VYOT) — I asked where he lives. Hearsay uses the same machinery with perception verbs, and the choice of word changes the meaning. There is also a hearsay frame with no named source at all: говорят (ga-va-RYAT — they say, people say) reports what is generally claimed rather than what a specific person said.
lessons.example: Build one report four times from one original utterance so that the differences are impossible to miss. Original: Я работаю в банке (ya ra-BO-ta-yoo v BAN-kye) — I work in a bank. Reported statement: Она сказала, что она работает в банке — She said that she works in a bank, with the present tense kept. Reported command: Она сказала, чтобы он работал в банке (SHTO-by on ra-BO-tal v BAN-kye) — She told him to work in a bank, where the second subject is nominative and the verb is past in form. Reported yes/no question: Она спросила, работает ли он в банке (a-NA spra-SEE-la, ra-BO-ta-yet lee on v BAN-kye) — She asked whether he works in a bank, with ли in second position after the focused word. Reported wh-question: Она спросила, где он работает — She asked where he works, with no particle. Now test hearsay. Я слышал, что она играет на гитаре (ya SLY-shal, shta a-NA ee-GRA-yet na gee-TA-rye) — I heard that she plays the guitar, is a report about a fact. Я слышал, как она играет на гитаре (kak) — I heard her playing the guitar, is a report about a perceived event, and Cornell prints exactly this contrast. Finally, break an English habit deliberately: the English sentence 'I asked if there was a meeting' must not become Я спросил, если было собрание, because если means 'in case', not 'whether'; the Russian is Я спросил, было ли собрание (BY-la lee sab-RA-nee-ye).
lessons.question: How do you report the question 'Will there be a meeting today?' in indirect speech, and where exactly does the joining word go?
lessons.answer: Будет ли сегодня собрание becomes Вы не скажете, будет ли сегодня собрание, with ли placed immediately after будет, the word being questioned.
lessons.distractor: The indirect form is Вы не скажете, если будет сегодня собрание, because English 'if' is translated by если in indirect questions.
lessons.correction: Если is reserved for conditional clauses and cannot mean 'whether'. Cornell's particle-ли page states the rule and prints the caution directly: ли is the word for 'whether', it comes right after the most important word of the question, and если, unlike English if, is used exclusively in conditional clauses. The same page shows the contrast in a minimal pair: Сегодня будет собрание? against Будет ли сегодня собрание?, where putting ли after будет keeps будет as the focus, and Сегодня ли будет собрание? would move the focus to сегодня. Position is meaning.

depth.definitions: Direct speech quotes an utterance; indirect speech reports it. Backshifting is the English habit of moving a reported verb one step into the past, as in he said he was tired from I am tired. A particle in this context is a short uninflected word that signals grammatical meaning rather than carrying a dictionary sense. Hearsay is information the speaker did not witness and is passing on. An indirect question is a question reported rather than asked.
depth.mechanism: Russian's reported speech is simpler in one respect and more explicit in another. It is simpler because tense is untouched: Wikipedia's article states that in Russian, as in many other Slavic languages, indirect speech uses the same verb tense as the equivalent sentence in direct speech, and it notes that the construction is the same for someone else's thought as for someone else's words, with examples such as Я думаю, что она красивая. It is more explicit because the joining word encodes what kind of utterance is being reported. Что reports a statement; чтобы reports a request, command or wish and switches the clause verb to a past form, as Cornell's page on чтобы shows with the meaning-changing pair сказать, что they signed against сказать, чтобы they sign; and ли reports a yes-no question, following the word under question, as Cornell's page on the particle demonstrates. Reported wh-questions need nothing because the question word is already present. Two limits are worth naming. First, ли is bookish: Cornell says the relaxed conversational way to ask a yes-no question is rise-fall intonation, so ли belongs mostly to indirect questions and to written questions. Second, the reported speech of an unverified source is not the same as a fact, which is why Russian separates слышал, что from слышал, как: the first reports content, the second reports a witnessed event.
depth.secondExample: Two reports of the same content, one about words and one about a witnessed event, then one report of a thought. Слышал, что: Я слышал, что он уехал в Москву (ya SLY-shal, shta on oo-YE-khal v Mask-VOO) — I heard that he has gone to Moscow, information from someone else. Слышал, как: Я слышал, как он уезжал (ya SLY-shal, kak on oo-yez-ZHAL) — I heard him leaving, an event the speaker perceived. Both are correct but they make different claims about evidence, and a careful reader notices which one a source used. Now a reported thought with the same tense treatment: Он думал, что она согласна (on DOO-mal, shta a-NA sag-LAS-na) — He thought that she agreed, with the present-tense short adjective left in place. Finally a reported request beside a reported statement: Он попросил, чтобы я позвонил (on pa-pra-SEEL, SHTO-by ya paz-va-NEEL) — He asked me to call, against Он сказал, что я позвонил — He said that I called. The difference in the report is the difference between being asked and being described.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first backshifts tense from English habit and produces reports whose verb is one step further back than the original. The second uses если for 'whether', turning an indirect question into a condition. The third uses что where a request is meant, converting a command into a statement and changing the meaning, as in сказал, что подписали against сказал, чтобы подписали. The fourth misplaces ли, attaching it to whatever word happens to be first rather than to the word being questioned, which moves the focus of the question. Diagnose by asking what kind of original utterance is being reported: statement, command, yes-no question, or wh-question. The kind of utterance selects the joining word and, for ли, the position.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: take five direct quotes from a news item or an interview in any language you can translate, and report each one in Russian, using at least one что clause, one чтобы clause, one ли question and one wh-question. Model response for one line: Он сказал, что работает в больнице, и спросил, будет ли собрание в пятницу (on ska-ZAL, shta ra-BO-ta-yet v bal-NEE-tse, ee spra-SEEL, BOO-dyet lee sab-RA-nee-ye v PYAT-nee-tsoo) — He said that he works at a hospital and asked whether there would be a meeting on Friday. Self-review rubric: (1) no tense was backshifted; (2) the joining word matches the type of utterance; (3) ли follows the word being questioned; (4) hearsay is presented as report rather than as established fact. The task is nonblocking.
depth.summary: Russian reports statements with что, requests and commands with чтобы plus a past form, yes-no questions with the particle ли placed after the questioned word, and wh-questions with no extra word at all. Tense is not backshifted, so a report preserves the original verb form, which is a genuine simplification once the habit of shifting is dropped. Hearsay is marked by the choice between reporting content and reporting a witnessed event.
