lessons.title: Hedging and politeness registers: ты, вы, and the words that lower the volume
lessons.explanation: A learner who knows the grammar of Russian can still sound blunt, because politeness in Russian lives in a small set of choices that carry no information at all. The first choice is the pronoun. Cornell's page on addressing people states the rule and then makes it operational: use вы (vy — you, polite or plural) and the form здравствуйте with people of greater age or status, such as a teacher, and use ты (ty — you, informal singular) with fellow students, and the page adds one rule of thumb that is worth memorising verbatim — use вы until you are advised otherwise, with the single exception of small children and teenagers, where вы is not appropriate in modern Russian. That is a register decision, not a grammatical one: both pronouns take the same verb endings in principle, but the whole social reading of the sentence changes. Spanish speakers already own this distinction between tú and usted, so the difficulty is not the concept but the boundaries, which do not map exactly. The second choice is the set of hedges that soften a claim or an offer. Наверное (na-VYER-na-ye — probably, I expect) qualifies a statement; может быть (MO-zhet byt — maybe) offers a possibility without committing; кажется (KA-zhet-sa — it seems) reports an impression rather than a fact; пожалуй (pa-ZHA-looy — I suppose, I am inclined to) signals a mild, deliberated yes; and вероятно (vee-ra-YAT-na — probably, in all likelihood) is the more formal relative of наверное. Spanish has a close parallel in quizás, tal vez, a lo mejor and al parecer, so the concept transfers, though the Russian words are used in different proportions and at different levels of formality. A third device is grammatical rather than lexical. Cornell records that the negative particle не in a question makes the question less abrupt or turns it into a request, as in Ты не знаешь, где живёт Аня? (ty nye ZNA-yesh, gdye zhee-VYOT A-nya) — Do you happen to know where Anya lives? The same page gives Извините, вы мне не поможете? — Excuse me, could you help me? Wikipedia's grammar article records the same habit in a table of answers to negative questions, where Не желаете ли печенья? is glossed 'Would you like to have some cookies?' with the note that negation is used only for more politeness. Two further softeners are worth knowing: the impersonal хочется (KHO-chet-sa — one feels like), which moves a want away from the speaker and makes it feel less like a demand, and the negated стать, which turns a refusal into a decision not to bother.
lessons.example: Take one request and lower its volume in five steps, then do the same for one opinion. Blunt imperative: Закрой окно (zak-ROY ak-NO) — Close the window. Add пожалуйста: Закрой окно, пожалуйста (pa-ZHA-loos-ta). Move to the polite pronoun and the -те form: Закройте окно, пожалуйста (zak-ROY-tye ak-NO, pa-ZHA-loos-ta) — Please close the window, addressing one person politely or several people. Add a negative frame: Вы не могли бы закрыть окно? (vy nye mag-LEE by zak-RYT ak-NO) — Could you possibly close the window? Add a hedge: Наверное, будет лучше закрыть окно (na-VYER-na-ye, BOO-dyet LOOT-she zak-RYT ak-NO) — It would probably be better to close the window. Now the same treatment for a want. Direct: Я хочу пойти в кино (ya kha-CHOO pay-TEE v kee-NO) — I want to go to the cinema. Softened: Мне хочется пойти в кино (mnye KHO-chet-sa pay-TEE v kee-NO) — I feel like going to the cinema, which Cornell glosses as the difference between 'I want' and 'I feel like'. Hedged further: Может быть, пойдём в кино? (MO-zhet byt, pay-DYOM v kee-NO) — Maybe we could go to the cinema? And a softened refusal: Я не стал спорить (ya nye stal SPO-rit) — I did not bother to argue, which Cornell records as the negated стать meaning 'won't take the trouble to'. Read the ten sentences in order and label each one's level: direct, polite, hedged, or impersonal. A prohibition shows the same dative-centred machinery in a formal setting: Здесь нельзя курить (zdyes neel-ZYA koo-REET) — You are not allowed to smoke here, where нельзя is a predicative and the person whose behaviour is at issue can be added in the dative.
lessons.question: A colleague you have just met asks you a question and you want to reply politely while signalling that you are not certain. Which two independent choices are you making, and what marks each one?
lessons.answer: A register choice with the pronoun — вы rather than ты, with the matching -те verb forms — and an epistemic hedge such as наверное or может быть attached to the content of the reply.
lessons.distractor: A single choice: adding пожалуйста to the sentence, which simultaneously marks the polite pronoun and expresses uncertainty.
lessons.correction: These are separate systems and they do not substitute for each other. The pronoun and the -те form mark the social relationship, as Cornell's ty-versus-vy page states with its rule of thumb to use вы until advised otherwise. The hedges mark how committed the speaker is to the content: наверное and вероятно rank a claim as probable, может быть offers a possibility, кажется reports an impression, and пожалуй signals an inclined assent. Пожалуйста is a courtesy marker for requests and offers; it says nothing about the relationship between the speakers and nothing about certainty. Getting the register right does not express doubt, and hedging does not express respect.

depth.definitions: Register is the level of formality a speaker chooses for a situation and a relationship. A hedge is a word or construction that reduces the strength of a claim or a request. Epistemic means relating to knowledge and certainty. An impersonal construction is one with no nominative subject, often with a dative experiencer, as in мне хочется. A particle is a short uninflected word expressing grammatical or pragmatic meaning.
depth.mechanism: Russian regulates politeness in three independent channels, and confusing them is the main source of unintended rudeness. The pronominal channel is binary and social: ты or вы, with вы plus -те forms as the safe default, as Cornell's page states, and with a documented exception for young children and teenagers. The particle channel is pragmatic: не in a question downgrades a demand into a request, which Cornell illustrates with Ты не знаешь, где живёт Аня? and Извините, вы мне не поможете?, and Wikipedia records the same effect in the question Не желаете ли печенья?, glossed as 'Would you like to have some cookies?' with the note that negation is used only for more politeness. The lexical channel is epistemic: наверное, вероятно, может быть, кажется and пожалуй each place the speaker at a different distance from the claim. Two further constructions belong to the lexical channel even though they are grammatical. The impersonal хочется, which Cornell describes as taking a dative person and meaning 'feel like' rather than 'want', removes the blunt first-person subject. The negated стать, which Cornell glosses as 'won't, won't bother to', packages a refusal as a decision not to act. A limit worth stating plainly: the ty/vy boundary is a social convention that varies by region and generation, and Cornell itself gives a rule of thumb rather than a law, so the only reliable method is to follow the other speaker's lead.
depth.secondExample: Read one declining sequence and watch which channel is doing the work. Я не знаю (ya nye ZNA-yoo) — I don't know, plain. Я не знаю точно (TOCH-na) — I don't know exactly, hedged by an adverb of degree. Наверное, я не знаю (na-VYER-na-ye, ya nye ZNA-yoo) — I probably don't know, hedged epistemically. Кажется, я не знаю (KA-zhet-sa, ya nye ZNA-yoo) — It seems I don't know, hedged by impression. Now put the same person in a formal setting: Я не уверена, что знаю это (ya nye oo-VYE-rye-na, shta ZNA-yoo EH-ta) — I am not sure that I know this, with the short adjective agreeing with the speaker. Cornell's short-adjective page shows that такие forms act as predicates with no present-tense verb, so неуверена carries 'am not sure' by itself. Read the four phrases and one formal version, and for each say which channel is at work: degree adverb, epistemic particle, or impersonal frame.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first uses ты with someone who expects вы, or forgets -те while using вы, which produces a mixed register that sounds careless rather than incorrect. The second piles up hedges until the sentence commits to nothing, as in Наверное, может быть, кажется, я не знаю, which reads as evasion rather than politeness. The third translates English 'please' into пожалуйста everywhere and expects it to carry politeness that Russian puts in the pronoun or the verb form. The fourth treats the negated question as a genuine denial, so that Вы не хотите кофе? is answered as though coffee had been refused, when the negative there is a politeness device. Diagnose by asking which channel the situation needs: relationship, commitment, or courtesy. Then choose exactly one marker from that channel rather than stacking several.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: write the same three messages — a request to a supervisor, a refusal to a friend, and an uncertain opinion about a plan — twice each, once plainly and once with the appropriate register markers, and label which channel you used each time. Model response for one line: plain Ты закроешь окно? against polite Вы не могли бы закрыть окно, пожалуйста? and hedged Наверное, лучше закрыть окно. Self-review rubric: (1) pronoun and verb form agree with each other; (2) exactly one hedge per uncertain claim; (3) any negative question was intended as politeness, not as a denial; (4) the register matches the relationship rather than the learner's preference. The task is nonblocking and involves no recording.
depth.summary: Politeness in Russian runs on three channels that never substitute for one another: the social pronoun choice of ты or вы with matching verb forms, the pragmatic use of не or ли to soften a question into a request, and the epistemic hedges that place the speaker at a distance from the claim. Impersonal constructions such as мне хочется and negated стать move the speaker out of the centre of the sentence. Because the ty/vy boundary is a convention rather than a rule, following the other speaker remains the safest method.

lessons.title: Idioms that resist word-for-word translation
lessons.explanation: Some Russian is not decodable. An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning cannot be recovered from its parts, and Russian has a large store of them that a learner meets long before the grammar is complete. The reason they matter here is diagnostic: each idiom is also a small fossil of grammar that no longer behaves productively, so recognising one saves you from trying to parse a sentence that does not want to be parsed. Take пять examples, each with its literal picture and its real meaning. Ничего себе (nee-chee-VO sye-BYE) looks like 'nothing to itself' and means something like 'wow' or 'no kidding', an interjection of surprise. Валять дурака (va-LYAT doo-ra-KA) looks like 'to roll a fool' and means 'to fool around, to mess about'. Бить баклуши (beet bak-LOO-shee) looks like 'to beat the blanks' and means 'to twiddle one's thumbs, to idle'; the баклуши were rough wooden blanks from which spoons were carved, so the picture is a job so easy it is barely work. Ни пуха ни пера (nee POO-kha nee pee-RA) looks like 'neither down nor feather' and is what you say to someone about to sit an exam, meaning 'good luck'; the traditional reply is к чёрту (k CHYOR-too — to the devil), literally sending the luck away so it is not jinxed. Руки не доходят (ROO-kee nye da-KHO-dyat) looks like 'hands do not reach' and means 'I never get round to it'. Two more idioms are so common they read as ordinary words until you notice their shape: не за что (NYE za shta), which literally asks 'not for what' and means 'you're welcome', and кстати (KSTA-tee), 'by the way', which is a fossilised prepositional form of a noun that no longer appears alone. Wiktionary documents each of these entries, and I cite it for the entry and the etymology only, with the caveat that it is a community dictionary and not an authority on usage. What ties the set together is a design feature worth naming: idioms preserve old case government, old participles and old lexical items, so they are evidence about the language rather than exceptions to it.
lessons.example: Read four idioms inside short dialogues and check that the literal reading fails. Ничего себе. — Я выиграла в лотерею. — Ничего себе! (ya VY-ee-gra-la v la-ta-RYE-yoo; nee-chee-VO sye-BYE) — 'I won the lottery.' 'Wow, no kidding!' Nothing is being said about anything belonging to itself. Валять дурака. — Хватит валять дурака, надо работать. (KHVA-teet va-LYAT doo-ra-KA, NA-da ra-BO-tat) — 'Stop fooling around, we have to work.' The verb валять here is not about rolling anything. Бить баклуши. — Он целый день бил баклуши. (on TSE-lyy dyen beel bak-LOO-shee) — 'He idled the whole day.' Note the past form бил, so the idiom inflects like an ordinary verb even though its meaning does not decompose. Ни пуха ни пера. — Завтра экзамен. — Ни пуха ни пера! — К чёрту! (ZA-vtra ek-za-MYEN; nee POO-kha nee pee-RA; k CHYOR-too) — 'The exam is tomorrow.' 'Good luck!' 'To the devil!' The reply is not rude; it is the expected ritual. Руки не доходят. — Ты прочитал эту книгу? — Нет, руки не доходят. (ty pra-chee-TAL EH-too KNEE-goo; nyet, ROO-kee nye da-KHO-dyat) — 'Have you read that book?' 'No, I never get round to it.' The hands are not the subject of a literal reaching, and the verb is plural with a plural noun. For each dialogue, say the literal translation aloud first and then the real meaning, because the gap between them is the whole point.
lessons.question: Someone says Ни пуха ни пера before your exam and you answer К чёрту. Why is that the correct reply rather than a rude one?
lessons.answer: Because ни пуха ни пера is a fixed good-luck formula and к чёрту is its traditional ritual answer, used to deflect the wish so that the luck is not jinxed; the exchange is idiomatic, not literal.
lessons.distractor: Because к чёрту is a neutral way of saying 'thanks' that can be substituted for спасибо in any situation.
lessons.correction: Idioms do not generalise. К чёрту belongs to this one ritual exchange and carries its meaning only inside it; using it as a general thanks would be strange and could sound genuinely rude, since the words themselves mean 'to the devil'. The correct reasoning is not that the words are polite but that the pair ни пуха ни пера and к чёрту is a fossilised exchange whose meaning is fixed by convention, exactly as 'bless you' follows a sneeze in English without being a theological statement.

depth.definitions: An idiom is a fixed multi-word expression whose meaning is not predictable from the meanings of its parts. A fossil is a form preserved in a fixed expression after it has stopped being produced freely elsewhere. Verb government is the set of cases and prepositions a particular verb requires. A calque is a literal translation of an expression from another language, which is exactly what produces unintelligible output with idioms.
depth.mechanism: Idioms are opaque for a structural reason, and naming it turns them from a memory burden into a reading strategy. Because an idiom is stored as a unit, its internal grammar stops being updated: валять in валять дурака and бить in бить баклуши retain a meaning and a government that the modern verb has lost, and кстати is a frozen prepositional form of a noun that survives nowhere else. That is why a learner who tries to parse an idiom will spend effort on a sentence whose grammar no longer composes. The same fossilisation is visible in the related expressions this course has already met. Cornell's page on себя notes that the word has no nominative form and refers only to the subject, which is why оно survives inside fixed uses; the page on 'each other' fixes друг друга as a unit that inflects like a masculine animate noun with prepositions inserted in the middle, as in друг с другом and друг к другу. Cornell's money page shows the same process inside ordinary vocabulary, where сдача and мелочь are two different words for two different senses of English 'change', a distinction English does not make and therefore cannot lend you. There is one honest limit: idiom meaning is conventional and sometimes regional, so a dictionary entry tells you what an expression means in standard usage but cannot guarantee it will be the right register in every situation. The same dependence on lexis rather than grammar appears in ordinary service Russian, where сдача is 'change' as an amount and мелочь is 'small change' as coins, as in Возьмите сдачу (vaz-MEE-tye ZDA-choo — Take your change) and У вас нет мелочи? (oo vas nyet MYE-la-chee — Do you happen to have any small change?).
depth.secondExample: Compare an idiom with a non-idiomatic collocation that looks structurally similar, because only one of them resists decomposition. Idiom: Он бил баклуши весь день means 'he lazed around all day' and cannot mean beating any physical object. Ordinary verbal phrase: Он бил молотком по гвоздю (on beel ma-lat-KOM pa gvaz-DYOO) — He was hitting a nail with a hammer, where every word means what it says and the instrumental marks the tool exactly as lesson 63 taught. Now a second pair. Idiom: руки не доходят, which has a fixed plural subject and a fixed meaning of procrastination. Ordinary phrase: Руки не достают до полки (ROO-kee nye das-ta-YOOT da POL-kee) — My hands don't reach the shelf, where the same noun and the same negative do compose literally. The practical test when reading is whether substituting a synonym for any single word destroys the meaning; if it does, you are looking at an idiom and should look it up whole rather than analyse it.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first translates an idiom word for word, which produces statements such as 'he beat the blanks' that carry no meaning. The second assumes an idiom is rude or formal when the ritual direction is the reverse, as with к чёрту. The third analyses the internal case government of an idiom and produces a correction where none is needed, such as repairing a perfectly standard друг с другом. The fourth generalises one idiom's register to other contexts, as when ничего себе is used to open a formal meeting. Diagnose by asking whether the meaning survives word substitution. If it does not, treat the phrase as one unit, look it up in a dictionary, and record its register alongside its meaning.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: collect five idioms you meet in reading or listening, and for each record four things: its literal picture, its real meaning, its register, and one sentence of your own using it. Model entry: бить баклуши — literally 'beat the blanks', means 'idle, goof off', informal; Он не любит бить баклуши, он всегда занят (on nye LYO-beet beet bak-LOO-shee, on vsyeg-DA ZA-nyat) — He does not like idling, he is always busy. Self-review rubric: (1) the literal gloss and the real meaning are both recorded and clearly different; (2) the register is named rather than guessed; (3) my own sentence keeps the idiom's fixed internal form; (4) I did not substitute a synonym inside the idiom. The task is nonblocking.
depth.summary: Idioms are stored whole, and that is why they resist parsing: their internal grammar is fossilised, so the parts no longer compose. Learn each one as a unit with a literal picture, a real meaning and a register, and treat the literal gloss as a memory hook rather than as a translation. The fossils themselves are evidence about the older state of the language, and the related fixed expressions such as друг друга and себя follow the same logic.

lessons.title: Telling a story with aspect contrast across a long narrative
lessons.explanation: Aspect is usually taught as a pair of labels, but across a whole narrative it becomes a way of organising information, and that organisation is what a reader actually tracks. Cornell's aspect page states the division plainly: the perfective expresses the end-point of an action and is used for events that are more specific and definite, while the imperfective describes actions without that end-point. In a story this maps onto a division of labour. The imperfective supplies the setting: what was going on, how things usually were, what a place looked like, what someone was doing when something happened. The perfective supplies the plot: the sequence of single, completed events that move time forward. Cornell's commentary on this is unusually clear, and it is worth keeping in the original spirit: the perfective is used for the specific instance and the imperfective for the same action done in general, as a matter of habit or principle, and the page notes that with adverbs such as всегда 'always' or часто 'often' the imperfective is required. A second mechanism governs negation, and Cornell is careful about how strong the rule is. The rough tendency is imperfective with negation, because what a speaker usually wants to convey is that the action was never started or never attempted: Он не брал мою книгу means 'He didn't take my book', not 'he failed to take it'. If the point is that something was attempted and failed, the perfective is the natural choice: Она не решила задачу means 'She didn't solve the problem', possibly after trying, while Она не решала задачу means 'She didn't work on the problem at all'. Cornell labels this a rough rule of thumb rather than a grammatical restriction, and that honesty matters. A third mechanism connects aspect to narrative questions: a question out of the blue, one that opens a topic with no shared presupposition, takes the imperfective, as in Вы читали этот роман? — 'Have you ever read this novel?', while a perfective version presupposes that the reading was expected and asks whether it is finished. Two further patterns complete the picture for long narratives. Cornell observes a statistical affinity between the imperfective and plural objects, and explicitly says this is a statistical fact rather than a grammatical rule, since perfective verbs take plural objects too. And time markers do real work alongside aspect: сначала (sna-CHA-la — at first), потом (pa-TOM — then), вдруг (vdroog — suddenly), наконец (na-ka-NYETS — finally), каждый день (KAZH-dyy dyen — every day).
lessons.example: Read one short narrative twice and mark the aspect of every verb before translating anything. Неделю назад я работал в маленьком офисе. Каждый день я приходил в девять и читал письма. В понедельник я пришёл, прочитал одно письмо и позвонил клиенту. (nee-DYE-lyoo na-ZAD ya ra-BO-tal v MA-lyen-kam A-fee-sye. KAZH-dyy dyen ya pree-kha-DEEL v DYE-vyat ee chee-TAL PEES-ma. v pa-nee-DYEL-neek ya pree-SHYOL, pra-chee-TAL ad-NO pees-MO ee paz-va-NEEL klee-YEN-too.) The first two sentences set the scene: работал and читал are imperfective, and каждый день forces the habitual reading, so no progress is claimed in time. The third sentence advances the plot: пришёл, прочитал and позвонил are all perfective, three bounded events in sequence. Now negate the middle of the story and watch the meaning shift. Я не читал это письмо (ya nye chee-TAL EH-ta pees-MO) — I did not read this letter, ever, is imperfective and denies that the action occurred at all. Я не прочитал это письмо (ya nye pra-chee-TAL) — I did not get this letter read, is perfective and implies the reading was expected or attempted. Finally, put the same content into a written compressed narrative: Прочитав письмо, он позвонил клиенту (pra-chee-TAF pees-MO, on paz-va-NEEL klee-YEN-too) — Having read the letter, he phoned the client, where the past deverbal adverb carries the first perfective event and the finite verb carries the second. Three sentences, three different aspect strategies, one story.
lessons.question: In the narrative Неделю назад я работал в офисе. Каждый день я приходил в девять. В понедельник я пришёл и позвонил клиенту, why does the writer use приходил in one sentence and пришёл in another?
lessons.answer: Приходил is imperfective and marks a repeated habitual routine, reinforced by каждый день; пришёл is perfective and marks one completed event on a particular day that moves the story forward.
lessons.distractor: Приходил is imperfective because the verb is in a subordinate role, and пришёл is perfective because a named day always requires the perfective.
lessons.correction: The trigger is the time phrase and the narrative function, not grammatical subordination or the mention of a day. Cornell states that with adverbs such as всегда the imperfective is required and that the specific instance takes the perfective; каждый день does the same work as всегда here, so the routine must be imperfective. Named days do not require the perfective — в понедельник я работал is perfectly normal if the point is what was going on that day. What forces пришёл is that the writer is presenting one bounded arrival as a step in a sequence, which is precisely the perfective's job of expressing an end-point.

depth.definitions: Aspect is the grammatical contrast between viewing an action as an ongoing, repeated or unbounded process and viewing it as a single bounded whole. Foreground in narrative is the chain of events that advances time; background is the setting, habits, descriptions and simultaneous states against which those events occur. End-point means the completion or boundary of an action. Presupposition is information a speaker assumes the listener already shares.
depth.mechanism: Aspect organises narrative because the two aspects answer different questions about the same event. The perfective answers 'what happened next', and the imperfective answers 'what was going on', 'what used to happen', and 'what was already true'. Cornell's aspect page sets the contrast as end-point against no end-point and warns explicitly that the general description is not a hard and fast grammatical rule that tells you exactly when to use one aspect and when the other, adding that the way to learn it is to note which aspect is used across a wide variety of circumstances, a process that takes experience. That warning is the honest centre of this lesson. Three sub-mechanisms follow from it. Negation has a tendency, not a rule: imperfective denies that an action occurred, perfective denies that it succeeded. Questions out of the blue take the imperfective because no presupposition exists, while perfective questions presuppose that the action was expected. Habit adverbs and habit expressions force the imperfective. Cornell's affinity claim about plural objects is explicitly statistical rather than grammatical, and it explains the pattern through real-world likelihood rather than syntax: when someone sets out to write a letter or finish a task, it is more often one thing than many. Two structural notes complete the picture: aspect is what makes the future available to perfective verbs, since a perfective verb with non-past endings expresses future time, and past deverbal adverbs are built from perfective verbs while present ones come from imperfective verbs, so aspect also decides which compressed narrative form is even available.
depth.secondExample: Compare two ways to narrate the same afternoon, one habit and one incident. Habit version: По выходным я вставал поздно, завтракал и читал газету (pa vy-khad-NYM ya vsta-VAL POZ-na, zaf-TRA-kal ee chee-TAL ga-ZYE-too) — At weekends I used to get up late, have breakfast and read the newspaper, all imperfective, no progress in time. Incident version: В субботу я встал поздно, позавтракал и прочитал газету (v soo-BO-too ya vstal POZ-na, pa-zaf-TRA-kal ee pra-chee-TAL ga-ZYE-too) — On Saturday I got up late, had breakfast and read the newspaper, all perfective, three bounded events. The content is identical and the aspect is doing the whole of the difference between a routine and one Saturday. Now insert a background clause into the incident: Когда я завтракал, зазвонил телефон (kag-DA ya zaf-TRA-kal, za-zva-NEEL tee-lye-FON) — While I was having breakfast, the telephone rang. The imperfective завтракал is an ongoing state, the perfective зазвонил is a single interrupting event, and the two aspects carry the whole relation between them with no extra word needed.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first narrates a sequence entirely in the imperfective, so the story describes but never advances. The second narrates everything in the perfective, producing a list of completed actions with no setting. The third treats the negation tendency as an absolute rule and rejects a perfectly normal perfective with a negative. The fourth assumes that a named time always forces the perfective, which is wrong because a named time can locate a background state. Diagnose by asking what each clause is doing: if it answers what happened next, the perfective is available; if it answers what was going on or what used to happen, the imperfective is the natural choice. Then check the time phrases, since habit adverbs and habit expressions override the other considerations.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: write a twelve-sentence narrative about a day that did not go as planned, with at least four imperfective verbs setting the scene, at least five perfective verbs carrying the events, one negated verb whose aspect you have chosen deliberately, and at least three time markers. Model opening: Утром шёл дождь, и я читал дома. Вдруг позвонил друг и попросил помочь (OOT-ram shyol dozhd, ee ya chee-TAL DO-ma. vdroog paz-va-NEEL drook ee pa-pra-SEEL pa-MOCH) — In the morning it was raining and I was reading at home. Suddenly a friend rang and asked for help. Self-review rubric: (1) background clauses are imperfective and event clauses perfective; (2) each negated verb's aspect matches whether the action failed or never started; (3) habit phrases take the imperfective; (4) the sequence is recoverable from the sentences without extra words. The task is nonblocking.
depth.summary: Aspect is the narrative's division of labour. The imperfective holds the background, the habits and the simultaneous states; the perfective carries the bounded events that move time forward. Negation follows a documented tendency rather than a rule, questions out of the blue take the imperfective, and habit phrases settle the choice before anything else does. Reading a long narrative means deciding, clause by clause, whether it is telling you what happened or telling you what was going on.

lessons.title: Reading a short text and holding five minutes about work and study
lessons.explanation: This lesson is where the level's tools stop being separate and become one reading and speaking routine. It has two halves. The first half is a short text written in the register of a real workplace profile. It is an authored model text composed for this course rather than a quotation from any external source, so the readings at the end point you to the grammatical references that explain its constructions rather than pretending it was reproduced from a publication. Here it is, with its own stressed pronunciation supplied in the item list: Меня зовут Ирина. Я работаю инженером в небольшой компании, которая строит мосты. Я закончила университет пять лет тому назад и с тех пор работаю здесь. Обычно я прихожу в офис в девять, проверяю письма и читаю отчёты. Мне нравится эта работа, хотя иногда она очень трудная. Сейчас я учусь на курсах, потому что хочу стать руководителем. Если всё будет хорошо, через год я получу диплом. In English: My name is Irina. I work as an engineer in a small company which builds bridges. I finished university five years ago and since then I have been working here. Usually I come to the office at nine, check the mail and read reports. I like this work, although sometimes it is very hard. At the moment I am taking a course, because I want to become a manager. If all goes well, in a year I will get a diploma. Read it with the toolkit in order. Find the relative clause with которая and decide its case. Find the profession expression работать инженером and note the instrumental, then compare with the nominative pattern Cornell records in response to Кем вы работаете. Find the participle-free construction but the gerund-free sequencing, and notice the aspect contrast between закончила, прихожу and читаю. The second half is a five-minute conversation about work and study, built as five one-minute turns. The conversation opens with the question Cornell records for this purpose, Кем вы работаете? (kyem vy ra-BO-ta-ye-tye — What do you do for a living?), and where age or time in a role matters the dative pattern appears, as in Сколько вам лет? (SKOL-ka vam lyet — How old are you?).
lessons.example: Use the model text as the input for the conversation, which is the real deliverable of the lesson. Turn one, identity and profession, one minute: Меня зовут Ирина. Я работаю инженером в небольшой компании (mee-NYA za-VOOT ee-REE-na, ya ra-BO-ta-yoo een-zhe-NYE-ram v nee-bal-SHOY kam-PA-nee) — My name is Irina, I work as an engineer in a small company. Turn two, history and duration, one minute: Я закончила университет пять лет тому назад и с тех пор работаю здесь (ya za-KON-chee-la oo-nee-veer-see-TYET pyat lyet ta-MOO na-ZAD ee s tyekh por ra-BO-ta-yoo zdyes). Turn three, routine and aspect, one minute: Обычно я прихожу в девять, проверяю письма и читаю отчёты — a habitual imperfective turn, with the routine marked by обычно. Turn four, purpose and opinion, one minute: Сейчас я учусь на курсах, потому что хочу стать руководителем (see-CHAS ya oo-CHOOS na KOOR-sakh, pa-ta-MOO shta kha-CHOO stat roo-ka-va-DEE-tye-lyem). Turn five, plans and hedging, one minute: Наверное, через год я получу диплом. Может быть, потом я буду работать в другом городе (na-VYER-na-ye, CHYE-ryez got ya pa-loo-CHOO dee-PLOM; MO-zhet byt, pa-TOM ya BOO-doo ra-BO-tat v droo-GOM GO-ra-dye). Rule for the five minutes: no turn may be a single sentence, every turn must contain at least one verb in each aspect, and at least one turn must report what another person said, using что or чтобы. If you get stuck, use a repair phrase and continue rather than stopping, as lesson 51 established. Two further sentences belong in the plan. A comparison: Это лучше, чем работа в банке (EH-ta LOOT-she, chem ra-BO-ta v BAN-kye) — This is better than working in a bank, which uses the short comparative better plus чем. And a repair phrase to keep the five minutes going when a word is lost: Повторите, пожалуйста (pav-ta-REE-tye, pa-ZHA-loos-ta) — Please repeat.
lessons.question: In the model text, why does the writer say Я работаю инженером rather than Я инженер, and when would the second version be the better choice?
lessons.answer: Работаю инженером uses the instrumental because инженер is a skilled or applied profession, which Cornell lists as acceptable with работать; Я инженер uses the nominative with no verb and is always acceptable too, and is the better choice when the profession is not a skilled trade, such as biologist, composer or professor.
lessons.distractor: Работаю инженером is required because all professions must follow работать in Russian, and the nominative version is an error.
lessons.correction: Cornell's professions page states the boundary rather than a blanket rule: работать plus the instrumental is used for skilled or applied professions such as врач, учитель, механик and журналист, while the nominative with no verb is used for other professions such as биолог, композитор and профессор, and it adds that the line between the two is not hard-and-fast and that the nominative construction is always acceptable, so Он врач is equivalent to Он работает врачом. The page also notes a partial English parallel: we say 'he works as a mechanic' but not 'he works as a philosopher'. So the choice is a register and category choice, not a correctness one.

depth.definitions: An authentic-style text is a passage written to match the register, sentence length and construction density of real published Russian, as distinct from a graded dialogue. A model text is one composed for teaching purposes and labelled as such. Reading strategy is the deliberate order in which a reader applies known tools to an unfamiliar passage. A conversation turn is one speaker's uninterrupted stretch of talk. A repair phrase is a fixed expression used to keep a conversation going when comprehension fails.
depth.mechanism: The point of reading a text of this kind is that the constructions are no longer presented one at a time, so the reader has to choose which tool to apply where. The model paragraph is deliberately built from this level's inventory. It contains a relative clause with которая, which requires naming the antecedent компания and then deciding whether the relative word is subject or object; a profession expression with the instrumental, which requires knowing Cornell's skilled-versus-other distinction; a duration expression with пять лет тому назад, which requires the accusative-plus-тому-назад pattern; a habitual imperfective sequence with обычно and прихожу, проверяю, читаю, which requires recognising repetition rather than events; a concession with хотя, which requires knowing that it introduces a clause rather than a phrase; a purpose clause with потому что, which requires distinguishing a reason from a presupposed cause; and a hedged future with наверное and через год, which requires the через-plus-accusative interval and an epistemic hedge. Cornell's sentence-type pages explain why the reading must be done structurally rather than word by word: mature Russian prose contains long sentences and varied word order, and the reader has to watch for the three kinds of predicate — verbs, short adjectives and predicatives, including o-forms — because sentence types without a nominative subject are normal in Russian rather than exceptional. That is the honest reason a learner can know every construction and still lose the thread of a paragraph.
depth.secondExample: Run the same reading strategy on a second short passage, of the same authored kind, to prove the routine transfers. Я студент. Я учусь в университете уже три года. Каждую неделю я сдаю экзамен или пишу работу. В прошлом году я сдал все экзамены, но не написал курсовую. Сейчас я пишу её и хочу закончить до лета, хотя работаю ещё и в кафе. (ya stoo-DYENT. ya oo-CHOOS v oo-nee-veer-see-TYE-te oo-ZHE tree GO-da. KAZH-doo-yoo nee-DYE-lyoo ya sda-YOO ek-za-MYEN EE-lee pee-SHOO ra-BO-too. v PROSH-lam ga-DOO ya sdal vsye ek-za-ME-ny, no nye na-pee-SAL koor-sa-VOO-yoo. see-CHAS ya pee-SHOO yeyo ee kha-CHOO za-KON-cheet da LYE-ta, kha-TYA ra-BO-ta-yoo ye-SHCHO ee v ka-FYE.) In English: I am a student. I have been studying at university for three years already. Every week I take an exam or write a paper. Last year I passed all the exams but did not write the coursework. Now I am writing it and want to finish before summer, although I also work in a café. The negation in не написал is perfective, so it reports a failure to complete rather than a refusal to start, which is the contrast lesson 79 established. The bare nominative Я студент and the instrumental-free profession statement show the other side of Cornell's professions pattern. Read both passages the same way and the routine is visible.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur when reading a real text. The first reads every clause as a main clause and never assigns the subordinate material, so the paragraph becomes a list of unconnected facts. The second uses the dictionary meaning of every word and ignores the aspect, which erases the difference between routine and event. The third treats a long sentence as unreadable rather than as a set of clauses to be labelled. The fourth, in speaking, produces one-sentence turns so that a five-minute conversation runs out in ninety seconds. Diagnose by asking, for each clause, whether it is a setting, an event, a relative description, a purpose or a concession, and then requiring that each spoken turn be built from at least three clauses with at least one of each aspect.
depth.application: Nonblocking task, two parts. Reading: take the model text and annotate it, labelling every relative clause, every case governed by a preposition, every aspect and every hedge; then do the same to the second passage without help. Speaking: hold a five-minute conversation about your own work and study, in five one-minute turns following the model. Model opening for turn one: Меня зовут ... Я работаю ... или Я учусь ... Self-review rubric, reading: (1) every relative clause has its antecedent named and its case justified; (2) every aspect is justified as routine or event; (3) each hedge is identified as epistemic rather than grammatical. Self-review rubric, speaking: (1) every turn lasts about a minute and contains at least three clauses; (2) each turn contains at least one imperfective and one perfective verb; (3) at least one turn reports someone else's words with что or чтобы; (4) I used a repair phrase rather than stopping when I lost a word. Both parts are nonblocking, and the conversation is assessed by the rubric rather than by a stream of binary questions, which are not evidence of proficiency.
depth.summary: The level ends where real use begins: a short text read structurally, with relative clauses, case government, aspect and hedging identified rather than guessed, and a five-minute conversation organised into turns that each carry a purpose, an aspect contrast and, in at least one case, reported speech. The tools of lessons 71 to 79 are not separate topics; they are the order in which a reader or speaker resolves an unfamiliar sentence.

readings.title: Cornell Beginning Russian Grammar — Professions
readings.note: Read the whole page. It gives Кем работает as the question for asking what a person does, states that работать plus the instrumental suits skilled or applied professions such as врач, учитель, механик, журналист and медсестра while other professions take the nominative with no verb, adds that the line between them is not hard-and-fast and that the nominative construction is always acceptable, notes the partial English parallel 'works as a mechanic' against 'works as a philosopher', and lists pairs where the term differs for a woman and a man, such as учитель and учительница. Note also the explicit comparison Он работает врачом beside Он врач.

readings.title: Cornell Beginning Russian Grammar — Sentence types: General comments
readings.note: Read the whole page; it is the case for reading structurally. It states that Russian has many major sentence types that are not a nominative subject plus verb, that three kinds of word make predicates — verbs, short adjectives and predicatives including o-forms — and that when reading mature Russian prose with its long sentences and varied word order you have to watch for these elements and recognise the type of sentence you are dealing with. It then reduces all long sentences to three structural types.

readings.title: Cornell Beginning Russian Grammar — Sentence types: structures with a Nominative subject
readings.note: Read the whole short page for the four patterns it lists: subject plus verb, subject plus short adjective for am/is/are, subject plus есть for existential statements such as У вас есть икра?, and subject with no verbal element at all, as in Саша здесь or Саша — врач. The last pattern is the one the model text's Я студент uses, and the third is the frame for talking about what an employer or a course provides.

readings.title: Cornell Beginning Russian Grammar — Sentence types: predicative (and no Nom. subject)
readings.note: Read the whole page. It explains that elements which correspond to English subjects are not nominative subjects in Russian, gives У нас нет икры and Мне холодно, and shows that tense is carried by было and будет because there is no nominative subject, with the paradigm Мне холодно, Мне было холодно, Мне будет холодно beside Надо делать упражнения, Надо было, Надо будет. It also gives Ясно, что у него большой талант, which shows a predicative running the main clause of a longer sentence.

readings.title: Cornell Beginning Russian Grammar — Two kinds of comparative
readings.note: Read the opening section. It states that short adjectives are used only as predicates while long adjectives can modify nouns as well, that the short comparative adds -ее to the stem and the long comparative puts более before the long adjective, that o-forms take the same short comparative, and that the adjective's stress pattern decides where stress falls, with the rule of thumb that polysyllabic stems have stem stress. The pair Саша умнее against Саша более умный человек is the pattern for comparing jobs and courses in the conversation.

readings.title: Cornell Beginning Russian Grammar — How old are you?
readings.note: Two lines, but useful for the conversation: it states that age is told with the dative case and prints Сколько тебе лет? with Мне девятнадцать лет. This is the pattern needed when a five-minute conversation about study touches on how long someone has been studying or how old they are, and it is the same dative-experiencer machinery as мне нравится and мне надо.

readings.title: Cornell Beginning Russian Grammar — The particle li
readings.note: Re-read the closing warning for the conversation's reporting section: ли is the word for 'whether' and is used mostly in indirect questions, and если must not be used for 'whether' because it is reserved for conditional clauses. The model text's final sentence uses a real condition with если всё будет хорошо, which is precisely the use if-based clause is reserved for.

readings.title: Wikipedia — Russian grammar, section 'Coordination'
readings.note: Read the opening paragraph for the three types of coordination and the conjunction lists. It states that conjoining coordination with и often expresses enumeration, simultaneity or immediate sequence and may also carry a cause-effect flavour, which is why the model text's sequence of finite verbs joined by и reads as a routine rather than as a chain of separate events. It also gives но, однако and зато for the opposition a concession may slide into.

visual.title: Read the paragraph in layers, then speak it back in turns
visual.description: A labelled two-part routine: a layered reading that labels every construction, followed by a five-turn speaking plan that reuses the same material about work and study.
steps: Skim the text once for its topic and for any unknown words, without stopping to resolve grammar.
Second pass, label the relative clauses: underline each который or которая, name its antecedent, and justify its case from its role in its own clause.
Third pass, label the case-governed phrases: mark every prepositional phrase and name the case the preposition requires.
Fourth pass, label the aspect of every verb as routine or event, and use habit words such as обычно and каждый день as the tie-breaker.
Fifth pass, label the hedges, the purpose clauses and the concessions, then restate the whole paragraph in two or three plain sentences.

For speaking, plan five one-minute turns — identity and profession, history and duration, routine with aspect contrast, purpose and opinion, plans with a hedge — and report one other person's words in at least one turn.

questions.prompt: An interview is reported as Он сказал, что работает врачом. A learner rewrites it as Он сказал, что работал врачом, believing the reporter must shift the tense. Which version matches Russian usage?
questions.answer: Он сказал, что работает врачом: Russian indirect speech keeps the tense of the original utterance, so a present-tense statement stays present inside a past-tense report.
questions.distractor: Он сказал, что работал врачом, because a past reporting verb always pulls the reported verb into the past, exactly as English does.
questions.correction: Wikipedia's indirect-speech section states that in Russian and many other Slavic languages indirect speech uses the same verb tense as the equivalent sentence in direct speech, and it prints Я не люблю шоколад beside Она сказала, что не любит шоколад with the literal gloss 'she said that she doesn't like chocolate'. The past is therefore the error, not the present. English backshifts out of habit, and a learner who trusts that habit will produce a report that sounds as though the working had already ended.

questions.prompt: You want to ask a colleague politely whether the report will be ready by Friday, and you want it to sound respectful rather than abrupt. Which sentence does the best job, and which two markers is it using?
questions.answer: Вы не могли бы сказать, будет ли отчёт готов к пятнице? — using the negative question frame and the particle ли to make an indirect question out of a yes-no question.
questions.distractor: Вы должны сказать, будет отчёт готов к пятнице? — using the obligation word and the plain word order to show that the answer matters.
questions.correction: Вы должны shifts the sentence from a request to an obligation and is the opposite of softening. Cornell records two separate devices for lowering the volume: the negative particle не, which makes a question less abrupt or turns it into a request, as in Извините, вы мне не поможете?, and the particle ли, which introduces an indirect yes-no question and follows the word being questioned, as in Вы не скажете, будет ли сегодня собрание? Wikipedia's grammar article adds that in Не желаете ли печенья? the negation is used only for more politeness. The two markers are independent, and neither is a statement about obligation.

questions.prompt: A colleague says Ты прочитал эту книгу? and you answer Нет, руки не доходят. What have you actually said, and why is a literal translation wrong?
questions.answer: You said 'No, I never get round to it'. Руки не доходят is a fixed idiom whose parts do not compose, so it reports procrastination rather than any physical reaching.
questions.distractor: You said 'My hands cannot reach it', meaning the book is stored somewhere you cannot get at, because the words are used with their ordinary meanings.
questions.correction: An idiom is stored as a unit, so its internal words stop carrying their ordinary sense. Cornell's page on друг друга shows the same property in a parallel expression: it is fixed as a unit, inflects like a masculine animate noun, and takes prepositions in the middle, as in друг с другом. The test when reading is whether substituting a near-synonym for one word destroys the meaning; if it does, the phrase must be learned whole and looked up rather than analysed. Here the fixed plural subject and the fixed meaning of procrastination both resist literal reading.

questions.prompt: In the narrative Вечером шёл дождь. Потом я пришёл домой, поужинал и прочитал письмо, which verb carries the background and which carry the plot, and what decided each choice?
questions.answer: Шёл is imperfective and sets the background scene, while пришёл, поужинал and прочитал are perfective and form the chain of completed events that moves the story forward.
questions.distractor: All four are perfective, because a story set entirely in the past must keep one consistent aspect throughout.
questions.correction: Cornell's aspect page divides the two by end-point: the perfective expresses the end-point of an action and suits specific, definite events, while the imperfective covers actions without that end-point, which is what a setting is. Nothing requires one aspect throughout, and a narrative that used the perfective for the weather would present the rain as a single bounded incident rather than as the condition the events happened in. The adverb потом marks the point where the narration moves from background to plot, and the aspect shift follows it.

questions.prompt: For a five-minute conversation about work and study, why is a plan of five one-minute turns with mixed aspect a better preparation than a list of forty single-sentence questions?
questions.answer: Because a turn is a stretch of real talk that must contain several clauses, at least one verb of each aspect and a purpose or concession, whereas single-sentence questions rehearse isolated forms and run out of material long before five minutes.
questions.distractor: Because five minutes is the maximum length a learner at this level can sustain, so the conversation must be cut short to match the turn count.
questions.correction: The turn structure is a design for producing connected speech, not a limit on it. The model text for this lesson contains a relative clause, an instrumental profession phrase, a habitual imperfective sequence, a concession and a hedged future, and each of those needs a clause of its own inside a turn. Cornell's sentence-type page explains why this matters for real use: mature Russian contains long sentences with varied word order and three different kinds of predicate, so the ability to hold several clauses together is the ability that reading and speaking both draw on. Binary recognition items are not evidence of proficiency, in Russian or anywhere else.

questions.prompt: A written report contains: Компания, основанная в 2010 году, сейчас строит новый мост, который соединит два района. Identify the two condensed constructions, say what each one replaces, and state which register each belongs to.
questions.answer: Основанная is a past passive participle inside a box construction, replacing the clause которую основали в 2010 году, and it belongs to written style; который соединит is a relative clause, the conversational equivalent of the participial compression.
questions.distractor: Основанная is a gerund describing the company's own action, and который соединит is a participle because it is attached to a noun.
questions.correction: Основанная has an adjective ending and agrees with компания in gender, number and case, which makes it a participle rather than a gerund; gerunds are indeclinable and take an -я or -в ending. Being built on a perfective verb with a past stem, it is a past passive participle, so the company receives the founding. Который соединит is a relative word agreeing with мост, exactly the structure Cornell describes when it says that который agrees with its antecedent in gender and number while taking its case from its own clause. Cornell's summary of the six deverbal forms states the register equivalence in one line: written style participles equal conversational style который clauses.

questions.prompt: Read the sentence Написав отчёт, она проверила данные, не говоря никому о проблеме. Explain the aspect and time relationship of each gerund, name the subject of both, and say why the third form is negative in form but not in meaning.
questions.answer: Написав is a past deverbal adverb built on a perfective verb, so the report was finished before the checking; не говоря is a present deverbal adverb built on an imperfective verb, simultaneous with the main action; both share the subject она, and не говоря means 'without saying' rather than denying anything.
questions.distractor: Написав means she is writing now and не говоря means she was not able to speak, because a past form must mean past time and a negative form must mean denial.
questions.correction: Cornell states that past and present in deverbal forms name the stem, not the time, and that the subject of a deverbal adverb is the subject of the main clause, so both forms belong to она and the writing finished first. The page on present deverbal adverbs records не говоря as a typical 'without -ing' usage, with the example Он стоял, ничего не говоря, which is why the negative here describes the absence of an action rather than contradicting one.

questions.prompt: A colleague explains: Мы не поехали на конференцию, потому что я заболел, хотя билеты были куплены. A learner translates the last clause as 'although the tickets were buying' and the main verb as 'we did not go, we refused to go'. Correct both errors and justify each.
questions.answer: Были куплены is a short-form past passive participle meaning 'had been bought', the completed state of the tickets, and не поехали with the perfective means the trip did not happen rather than a refusal, which would more naturally be expressed with a different verb or construction.
questions.distractor: Были куплены is an imperfective past verb meaning 'were buying', and не поехали means 'we declined to go' because a negated perfective always denies an attempt.
questions.correction: A form in -ны with the copula были is the short past passive participle, which reports a resulting state rather than an action in progress, and Cornell's six-deverbal-forms page lists the short forms of past passive participles among the forms that also occur conversationally. For the negation, Cornell's trying-and-failing page states the tendency the other way round and calls it a rough rule of thumb: the imperfective is the natural choice when the point is that the action never started, so не поехали reports that the trip did not occur, while a denial of attempted failure would be a different choice. Neither reading supports a claim about refusal.

questions.prompt: Compose a four-clause report of a meeting so that it contains one what-clause, one request-clause, one question about whether something happened, and one concession. State for each which joining word you chose and why, and confirm that no tense was backshifted.
questions.answer: Use что for the statement, чтобы with a past form for the request, ли after the questioned word for the yes-or-no question, and хотя for the concession; the tense of every reported verb stays as it was in the original utterance.
questions.distractor: Use что for all four, since Russian has a single reported-speech particle and the difference in English comes only from intonation.
questions.correction: Russian encodes the type of utterance in the joining word. Wikipedia's indirect-speech section states that Russian indirect speech keeps the tense of the original sentence, and Cornell's pages supply the rest: что introduces a reported statement, чтобы with a past form introduces a request or command and changes the meaning when swapped with что, as in сказать, что they signed against сказать, чтобы they sign, ли introduces an indirect yes-or-no question and follows the word being questioned, and хотя introduces a concession as a full clause. If a single particle covered all four, the meaning-changing pair Cornell prints could not exist.

questions.prompt: Choose the right completion: Я приехал в Москву (а) неделю, (б) через неделю, (в) неделю тому назад, when the intended meaning is 'I arrived in Moscow a week ago'. Explain what each of the other two options would mean.
questions.answer: Option (в), неделю тому назад, gives 'a week ago'; option (а) неделю alone would mean he arrived for a stay of a week, a duration; option (б) через неделю would point forward and mean 'I will arrive in a week' or 'a week later'.
questions.distractor: Option (б) через неделю, because через plus the accusative is the general Russian equivalent of English 'in' with time words and therefore covers past as well as future.
questions.correction: Cornell's elapsed-time page shows через pointing forward from a reference point, in Я это сделаю через неделю and Он приехал через неделю, 'a week later', and the duration page shows the bare accusative measuring, in я была там неделю. The ago page then states that тому назад follows the accusative unit of time and that тому is optional, giving неделю назад. Three shapes, three meanings, and only the third reaches back from now.

questions.prompt: You must ask a professor, whom you have just met, for a small favour, then decline a colleague's invitation informally, then report both to a friend. Which register markers do you use in the first two, and which joining word appears in the third?
questions.answer: With the professor, вы plus the -те verb form and a softened request frame such as Вы не могли бы …; with the colleague, ты plus a plain informal form; and when reporting to the friend you introduce the reported content with что, or чтобы if you are passing on a request.
questions.distractor: Use пожалуйста in both first two sentences, since пожалуйста alone carries the register, and report with ли because ли marks any indirect speech.
questions.correction: Пожалуйста is a courtesy marker for requests and offers and does not encode the relationship, and ли marks an indirect yes-or-no question rather than reported speech in general. Cornell's ty-and-vy page states the pronoun rule with its rule of thumb to use вы until advised otherwise and its exception for young children, and its particle-не page shows the softened request frame. For reporting, Cornell's чтобы page and Wikipedia's indirect-speech section both work from the kind of utterance: a statement takes что, a request takes чтобы with a past form.

questions.prompt: Rewrite as a single compressed written sentence: Я прочитал статью, потом я написал отчёт, и после этого я позвонил клиенту. Then say which aspect each compressed form carries and why the compression is appropriate in written style.
questions.answer: Прочитав статью, я написал отчёт и позвонил клиенту, where прочитав is a past deverbal adverb carrying the first perfective event and написал and позвонил are perfective finite verbs carrying the chain.
questions.distractor: Читая статью, я писал отчёт и звонил клиенту, because the imperfective covers more than one action and compresses better.
questions.correction: Читая and писал would present the reading and writing as overlapping or habitual, which reverses the sequence and loses the end-points. Cornell states that past deverbal adverbs are formed on the past stem of a perfective verb and that they are used mostly in written style, and it gives the minimal pair Он сидел за столом, читая газету against Прочитав газету, он ушёл. The first is simultaneous and imperfective, the second sequential and perfective, and only the second matches a narrative of three completed steps.

questions.prompt: A learner writes Нож, которая лежит на столе, мой for 'The knife which is lying on the table is mine'. Diagnose the error, supply the correct form, and state the two features a relative word takes from two different places.
questions.answer: The form should be который, because нож is masculine singular; the relative word takes gender and number from its antecedent and case from its function in its own clause, which here is nominative as the subject of лежит.
questions.distractor: The form should be которую, because the relative word takes the case of the noun phrase it modifies and нож is the object of the whole sentence.
questions.correction: Cornell states the rule in a single sentence on the kotoryj page: the word agrees with its antecedent in gender and number, but its case depends on its function in its own clause. Under that rule нож supplies masculine singular, ruling out которая, and лежит supplies the nominative because the relative word is its subject. Taking case from the antecedent would produce в который we live-style errors, which the same page's examples guard against.

questions.prompt: You have two minutes to tell a story about a journey that went wrong, and you want the listener to hear both the setting and the events. Plan the aspect distribution and name four time markers you would use.
questions.answer: Open and close the setting in the imperfective — what the weather was like, what you were doing, what usually happens — and carry the events in the perfective, one bounded verb per step; use сначала, потом, вдруг and наконец to mark the sequence.
questions.distractor: Use the perfective for everything so that every sentence reports a completed event, and rely on the time markers alone to distinguish the setting from the plot.
questions.correction: An all-perfective story turns the setting into a list of incidents and loses the background that makes events meaningful. Cornell's aspect page divides the two by end-point, with the perfective for specific and definite events and the imperfective for actions without an end-point; the habit page adds that adverbs such as всегда and часто require the imperfective, which is exactly the language of setting. The page on questions out of the blue is a further reminder that aspect carries presupposition as well as time, so the listener's expectations depend on the choice.

questions.prompt: Someone offers you a lift and you want to accept, but you are only fairly sure it will suit. Name the register decision and the hedging decision separately, then give one sentence that carries both without stacking markers.
questions.answer: The register decision is the pronoun and verb form, ты with an informal form or вы with -те depending on the relationship; the hedging decision is a single epistemic marker such as наверное or пожалуй attached to the content, as in Спасибо, наверное, я поеду с вами.
questions.distractor: The register decision is to add пожалуйста, and the hedging decision is to add кажется and может быть together so that the uncertainty is unmistakable.
questions.correction: Politeness and hedging run on separate channels and never substitute for each other: пожалуйста is a courtesy marker for requests and offers, while наверное, вероятно, может быть, кажется and пожалуй each place the speaker at a distance from the claim. Cornell's ty-and-vy page governs the first decision, and its khotet'-versus-khotet'sya page shows the same separation in the impersonal softener, glossing Мне хочется as 'I feel like' against Я хочу as 'I want'. Stacking two hedges makes the speaker sound evasive rather than careful.

questions.prompt: Read the minute of a meeting: Обсудили проект. Сначала мы спорили о сроках. Потом решили, что отчёт должен быть готов к пятнице, и директор попросил, чтобы все проверили свои части. Label every construction that this level has taught, and say which clause reports a command.
questions.answer: Обсудили is a concrete instance in the perfective; спорили is imperfective background; решили is a bounded decision; отчёт должен быть готов is the short adjective должен with a nominative subject and an infinitive; and к пятнице is a future deadline with к plus the dative. The command is reported by попросил, чтобы все проверили, using чтобы with a past form because the subjects differ.
questions.distractor: The command is reported by решили, что отчёт должен быть готов, because что introduces requests as well as statements when the verb is a verb of decision.
questions.correction: Что introduces a reported statement, so решили, что отчёт готов reports what was decided, whereas попросил, чтобы все проверили passes on a request addressed to different people. Cornell's chtoby page makes this contrast explicit with the meaning-changing pair сказать, что they had signed against сказать, чтобы they sign, and states that when the two verbs have different subjects the construction must be чтобы plus an л-form. The должen pattern comes from the page on должен, which states that with it the person is nominative, in contrast with the dative person required by надо.

questions.prompt: For a five-minute talk about work and study, list four constructions you must deploy and explain what each one tests, then state one thing the assessment cannot show.
questions.answer: A profession statement with работать plus the instrumental tests the skilled-versus-other profession distinction; a relative clause with который tests the two-agreement rule; a reported request with чтобы tests subject identity; and a hedged future with через plus the accusative and an epistemic marker tests interval and register together. The talk cannot show general proficiency, because five minutes of planned speech is a rehearsal of specific constructions rather than evidence of fluency.
questions.distractor: A profession statement, a listing of ten noun cases, a memorised proverb and a request for feedback, which together show grammatical mastery of the whole course.
questions.correction: Cornell's professions page documents the работать-versus-nominative boundary and calls the line between them not hard-and-fast; the kotoryj page supplies the two-agreement rule; the chtoby page supplies the two-subject rule; and the time pages supply через plus the accusative and тому назад. Reciting case names and memorised idioms tests recall rather than use, and no set of recognition items or a single recorded talk can establish general proficiency. That limit is stated rather than papered over, because overclaiming is the failure mode this level is designed to avoid.
